en: The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha, with your mind attached to Me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me, [you shall attain perfection].
Listen to how you shall know me completely and without doubt. 1.
Śrīdhara:
The reality of the self has been explained, as well as its conjunction [with the material world].
Now, the divine form which is to be worshipped is being described.
At the end of the previous chapter, it was said: "He who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me is considered by Me to be the most perfectly integrated.
Here, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of person you are to whom devotion should be offered, the Blessed Lord, intending to describe His own true nature, said: "In Me" (mayi).
This refers to one whose mind is attached to and fixed upon Me, the Supreme Lord.
"Having me as his support" means one for whom I alone am the support; being one who has no other refuge,
while practicing yoga— that is, performing repeated cultivation— he will undoubtedly attain it in this very way.
Listen to this which I shall speak, so that you may know me in my entirety, together with my manifestations, powers, sovereignty, and so forth. //1//
Madhusūdana:
I bow to that Śrī Nandana, the mass of supreme bliss, without devotion to whom there is no liberation, and who is the one to be served by all yogis.

Thus, having explained the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou") along with its yoga, by means of the first hexad which primarily concerns the practice consisting of the renunciation of action (*karma-saṃnyāsa*),

the meaning of the term *tat* (the "that") must now be explained by means of the middle hexad, which primarily propounds the Brahman that is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*). Within that [middle hexad] as well—
"The one among all yogis who, with his inner self absorbed in Me, worships Me with faith— he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined" (Gītā 6.47).
With this, the seventh chapter begins as an explanation of the worship of the Blessed One mentioned previously.

In this regard, Arjuna ought to have asked two things: what kind of form of the Blessed One is to be worshipped, and how one’s inner self (antarātman) becomes absorbed in that [form]. Yet, out of supreme compassion, the Blessed Lord, wishing to speak of these two matters even though they had not been asked, said: "In Me" (*mayi*).

"In Me"—that is, in Me, the Supreme Lord, who possesses manifold glories such as being the abode of the entire universe—refers to you, whose mind is attached to Me, meaning it is always fixed upon Me through the abandonment of all other objects.

Therefore, one who has me as his refuge and me alone as his shelter; whereas it is well known that a king’s servant takes refuge with the king and has his mind attached to his wife and so forth, a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), however, has me as his refuge and his mind attached to me. You, or someone like you, practicing yoga—that is, performing the concentration of the mind in the manner described in the sixth chapter—[should do so].
Listen as I speak of how you shall come to know me— without doubt, in my entirety, and endowed with all sovereign power, strength, capacity, majesty, and so forth— in what manner,
O Viśvanātha,
[you shall know] the Great Lord, the source of eternal bliss.
We take refuge at the feet of the ocean of the nectar of compassion, so that, having utterly abandoned both liberation and its path,
we may attain the nectar of divine love by way of devotion.
In the seventh [chapter], the sovereignty of the venerable Kṛṣṇa, who is worthy of worship, is described;
those who do not worship Him and those who do worship Him are also stated to be of four kinds.

In the first group of six chapters, the paths of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*)—which depend upon desireless action for the purpose of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) and which bring about the fruit of liberation—were described. Now, by means of this second group of six chapters, [the author describes] that which brings about the fruits of *sālokya* and other states through both desirelessness and desire based on hearing [the scriptures] mixed with action, knowledge, and so forth; furthermore, that which is the supreme among all, being independent of action, knowledge, and the like, and which brings about the fruit of liberation characterized by becoming an attendant (*pārṣada*) out of love.

Thus, as stated in passages such as, "Whatever is attained through ritual acts, whatever through austerity, and whatever through knowledge and dispassion," and "My devotee attains all of this directly through the yoga of devotion to Me— both heaven and liberation, and My own abode" (BhP 1.20.32–33)— [the devotee] is the accomplisher of all goals, including heaven and liberation, even without any subsequent means of practice.
Furthermore, the glorious Bhakti-yoga is said to be supreme, independent, easy for all to perform, yet difficult for all to perform.
But surely, based on the Vedic scripture, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8), you must ask:
how can there be liberation through devotion alone, without knowledge?

Not so; the meaning of this Vedic scripture is that one transcends death only by knowing and directly experiencing that very referent of "That" (tat-padartha), which is the Supreme Self (paramātman) itself—not by knowing the referent of "thou" (tvam-padartha), nor the individual self (ātman), nor primordial nature (prakṛti), nor even mere material objects.

In this regard, just as the tongue alone is the cause for perceiving the taste of white sugar and not the eyes, ears, or other senses, so too the perception of Brahman, who is beyond the qualities (guṇātīta), is possible [only through such direct experience].
It is not, however, through the sāttvika knowledge of a self distinct from the body and so forth;
for the Blessed One has declared, "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone" (BhP 11.14.11).
We shall explain with specific details in the passage, "By devotion one comes to know Me truly, as who I am and how great I am" (Gītā 18.55).
The well-known status of knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga as means to liberation, however, exists solely due to the influence of devotion (*bhakti*), which remains subordinate within them;
for it is heard repeatedly that without it, those two are ineffective.
Furthermore, because the particle *eva* is not employed immediately after the word *viditvā* in this scriptural passage,

once it is made known that there is no exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of connection [with the unknown], the meaning obtained is that liberation results from that very Supreme Self, whether known or even in some cases unknown.
And from that, liberation arises through the knowledge of the Supreme Self, which is devoid of qualities and born of devotion.
However, in some cases, the meaning culminates in the conclusion that liberation occurs even without that knowledge born of devotion, by devotion alone;
just as a disease destroyed solely by sugar-candy is surely cured even when the candy is eaten without its sweetness being perceived due to a defect in the sense of taste—of this there is no doubt.
"Matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa-vikāra, śarkarā, and sitā" are synonyms for sugar, according to Amara.
It was said by the illustrious Uddhava: "Indeed, the Lord [bestows His grace] even upon the ignorant who worship Him directly..."
"It spreads the highest good like a sovereign medicine when consumed" (BhP 10.47.56).

Also, in the eleventh book it is said: "Whatever is attained through ritual actions, whatever through austerity, and whatever through knowledge and dispassion—in all these, my devotee attains everything directly by means of the yoga of devotion to Me" (BhP 11.20.31–32).
Therefore, by many such statements beginning with "even a Pukkasa is liberated from saṃsāra by hearing my name even once," it is established that liberation comes through devotion alone.
Now, let us return to the subject at hand:
"Of all yogis as well, he whose inner self is absorbed in Me..."
"Whosoever, full of faith, worships Me, he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined" (Gītā 6.47).

By this statement of Yours, it is understood that You have defined the specific characteristic of Your own particular devotee as being "possessed of faith directed toward Your person," provided that his mind is fixed on You.

However, in response to the inquiry as to what kind of devotee such a person is and who is qualified for his knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), You say in two verses beginning with "attached to Me. Although—
Devotion to the Supreme Lord, the experience of Him, and detachment from everything else— these three occur simultaneously for one who takes refuge,
just as they occur in one who is eating.
As it is said: "Contentment, nourishment, and the removal of hunger occur with every morsel," the sequence of experiencing Me occurs precisely from the beginning of the process of worship;
yet, for one who eats even only a single morsel, such contentment and nourishment do not become manifest.
But you shall know me only as one who eats many morsels of food;
likewise, you shall know me only when your mind is attached— having ascended to the stage of intense attachment— to me, Śyāmasundara, clad in yellow garments,
such that you will experience me clearly.

Listen to what kind of yoga that is: one who, practicing union with Me, gradually attains Me as his sole refuge—meaning one who takes refuge in Me alone and not in knowledge, action, or the like, being a devotee of no other.
By the two words "here" (*atra*) and "without doubt, entirely" (*asaṃśayaṃ samagram*), [it is indicated that] the knowledge of My nature as the non-dual Brahman is intended.
"Affliction is greater for those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest,
for the goal of the Unmanifest is attained with difficulty by embodied beings"—
because of this statement that follows, [the path] is indeed accompanied by doubt.
Likewise, that Brahman which is to be worshiped by the wise is the very nature of My own glory, who am the Supreme Greatness.
As was said by Me alone in the form of a fish to Satyavrata:
"My own glory is designated by the term 'Supreme Brahman'."

"You shall know that which has been favored by me and revealed through my questions within your heart" (BhP 8.24.38). Here too, it is indicated by the statement "For I am the foundation of Brahman" (Gītā 14.27) that my knowledge is not complete. //1//
Baladeva: In the seventh [chapter], the sovereignty of the Object of Worship over himself is proclaimed,
as well as the fourfold nature of those who worship Him and likewise of those who do not.
By the first group of six verses, the nature of the living being as a worshiper and the means for attaining Him are primarily described.
By the middle group, however, those very qualities of the Self who is the object of worship are likewise stated.
In that context, what is the nature of Your worshipable form indicated at the end of the sixth verse?
"How might the inner self of one who worships become absorbed in That?"— desiring to speak of this even though it was not asked by Pārtha, the Blessed One, out of compassion, said "In Me" (*mayi*).
You, or anyone else, whose mind is attached to Me— the object of worship whose characteristics have been explained— and who is exceedingly devoted to Me,
such a person, taking Me as their refuge through any one of the dispositions such as servitude or friendship, attains *yoga*.
Applying the characteristics of being my devotee and so forth, he has set out to act;
"without doubt" means that he is free from uncertainty as to whether Kṛṣṇa alone is the supreme reality or something else, and thus possesses the certainty of my own preeminence— this is the meaning.

O Pārtha, listen with an attentive mind to that which is being spoken by Me— the knowledge by which you shall know Me, the Lord of All, in My entirety, together with My abode, My manifestations, and My attendants.
Nor should it be said that he teaches knowledge in its entirety—that is, in its fullness—for such complete knowledge is impossible for him who is infinite;
and as for memory, even one who is unborn is not able to express it in its entirety.
I shall declare to you this knowledge along with realization in its entirety;
having known which, nothing further remains here to be known. //2//

Śrīdhara: He praises the knowledge about to be described with the words "Knowledge" (jñānam). Knowledge consists of scriptural learning (*śāstrīya-vijñāna*) and realization (*anubhava*). Accompanied by that, I shall speak this [knowledge] concerning Me in its entirety, that is, in its fullness.
The meaning is that once this has been known, for one abiding on the path to the highest good, there remains nothing further to be known;
by that alone, one's purpose is fulfilled. //2//

Madhusūdana: By saying "you shall know," he praises [the knowledge] with the word "knowledge" (*jñānam*) in order to direct the listener's attention, thereby dispelling the doubt that such knowledge might be merely indirect (*parokṣa*).
This knowledge concerning Me is inherently direct (*aparokṣa*);
however, because it fails to produce its fruit due to obstacles such as incredulity (*asambhāvanā*), it is figuratively called "indirect" until those obstacles like incredulity have been removed.

However, at the conclusion of the maturation of inquiry, the knowledge produced by that very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), being free from obstruction, produces its fruit and is called "immediate" (aparokṣa).
And because it is perfected through the maturation of inquiry, that very consciousness—

this immediate knowledge arising from the scripture accompanied by that consciousness— I, your supreme authority, shall declare to you in its entirety, including the means and the fruits, without any remainder.
I shall explain.

Following the Vedic declaration that through the knowledge of one thing there comes the knowledge of all things, he says: having known that knowledge which is of the nature of eternal consciousness, and having made it the object of a mental modification (*mano-vṛtti*) produced by the Vedanta, [one realizes] that here on the plane of worldly transaction, there is never again anything else.
Not even the slightest thing remains to be known.

Since all imagined things are sublated by the knowledge of "Being-only" (sanmātra), which is the substratum of everything, and only "Being-only" remains, the intention is that you will achieve your goal through the knowledge of that alone. //2//
Viśvanātha: In that regard, even prior to the stage of attachment (*āsakti*) to my devotion, my knowledge shall consist of majesty (*aiśvarya*);
thereafter, my realized wisdom (*vijñāna*) shall consist of the experience of sweetness (*mādhurya*).
"Listen to both of these," he says with the words beginning "knowledge" (*jñānam*).

The meaning is that there is nothing else to be known that is not distinguished [from this]; thus, even in the knowledge and realization of Brahman as non-different from Me, this very [knowledge] is included within it. //2//

Baladeva: He praises the knowledge about to be described with the words "Knowledge. This knowledge concerns the essential nature of the Lord who possesses the powers of cit (consciousness) and acit (matter). And that, along with realized wisdom (vijñāna), I shall declare.

The meaning is this: I shall teach you—who have surrendered with complete and total completeness—that knowledge (*vijñāna*) which has as its object the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as distinguished from those two powers;

that is, the knowledge whose objects are both that essential nature which is the cause of all and that which is to be meditated upon. This knowledge, by knowing which, nothing further remains to be known for you, the seeker who has entered the path to the highest good (*śreyas*).
Because everything is included within that. //2//
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and have attained perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth. (7.3)
Śrīdhara: He says "of men" (manuṣyāṇām) to show that knowledge which is difficult to attain without devotion to Me.

Among the innumerable living beings, those other than humans do not even have the inclination toward their own highest good. But among thousands of men, only someone here or there, by the power of merit, strives for the perfection of self-knowledge.
Even among thousands who exert effort, only someone rare comes to know the Self by virtue of preeminent merit;
and even among thousands of such knowers of the Self, only someone rare knows Me, the Supreme Self, in truth through My grace.
Thus, the meaning is that I shall declare to you that knowledge which is exceedingly difficult to attain. //3//
Madhusūdana: And this knowledge, which yields great fruit, is extremely difficult to attain without my grace;
for it is said, "among men.

Among thousands of men who are fit for scriptural knowledge and action, perhaps only one—having achieved discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities through the accumulation of merit performed over many births—[attains it].
He strives; he exerts himself for the sake of perfection, for the arising of knowledge by means of the purification of the mind.

Among those who strive—that is, among those practitioners who have exerted themselves and achieved success through previously acquired merit—even one among them, at the conclusion of the ripening of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption, knows Me, the Lord, and realizes Me directly.

The meaning is this: from the great Mahāvākyas taught by the Guru, such as "Thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*), which [reveal] reality through its non-difference from the inner self (*pratyag-abheda*) in its true nature;
among many men, one who practices the means for the knowledge of the Self is extremely rare.
Among those who do practice the means, it goes without saying that one who partakes of the fruit is extremely rare—such is the intended sense regarding the majesty of this knowledge. //3//

Viśvanātha: Stating that this "conscious knowledge" (*sa-vijñāna*)—which is my own knowledge and which is difficult even for those possessing knowledge or those who are yogis to attain according to the characteristics previously described in the first six chapters—he first speaks of "conscious knowledge" with the words "of men" (*manuṣyāṇām*). Among the innumerable living beings (*jīva*), only some rare one becomes a human being.
Among thousands of men, only one strives for the highest good;

and among thousands of such men, only one truly knows me in my form as Śyāmasundara and experiences me directly. The bliss of experiencing the Brahman with attributes (saviśeṣa-brahmānubhavānanda) is a thousand times greater than the bliss of experiencing the attributeless Brahman (nirviśeṣa-brahmānubhavānanda).
The intended meaning is "it might be so. //3//
Baladeva says: He speaks of the rarity of one's own knowledge with the words "of men" (*manuṣyāṇām*).

Among the countless living beings (*jīvas*) who possess various and diverse natures, only a few are human beings; and among thousands of those humans who are qualified for the study of the scriptures, only a rare individual strives for perfection—that is, for the realization of his own and the Supreme Self—by virtue of association with the saintly (*sat-prasaṅga*).
But not everyone.

Among thousands of such persons who strive, who exert themselves, who have attained perfection, and who have gained the vision of both their own self and the Supreme Self, only one truly knows Me, Kṛṣṇa, in essence.

This is the meaning: many people who practice the teachings of the scriptures, having experienced the atomic consciousness of their own selves as a mere fragment of space and as a portion of Myself—the Supreme Self—are liberated.
But someone who has attained devotion to Me through such association with the virtuous truly knows Me, Kṛṣṇa, now as the suckling of Yaśodā and your charioteer;

that is to say, he experiences Me as the perfect Brahman, possessing inconceivable and infinite power, being the cause of all, an ocean of countless jewels of auspicious qualities such as omniscience, universal sovereignty, and affection for My devotees.
And that Great-Souled One will say: "He is very difficult to find" (Gītā 7.19), and "But no one knows me" (Gītā 7.26). //3//
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego— thus is My nature divided eightfold. (7.4)

Śrīdhara: Having thus directed the listener's attention, he now speaks in two verses beginning with "bhūmiḥ" regarding the two-fold *prakṛti*—distinguished as the higher and the lower—in order to define the reality of the Lord (*īśvara-tattva*) as the agent of creation and so forth through the medium of *prakṛti*. By the words "earth" and so on, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), such as smell and the rest, are expressed.
By the word "mind" (manas) is meant the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is its cause;
by the word "intellect" (buddhi) is meant the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva), which is its cause; and by the word "ego-sense" is meant ignorance (avidyā), which is its cause.
Thus, [the subtle body] is divided eightfold.
Alternatively, by the words "earth" and so forth, the five great elements are understood together with their subtle counterparts;
by the word "ego-sense" (ahaṅkāra), the ego itself is meant, and by that very term its effects—the sense organs—are also included;
and "intellect" (buddhi) refers to the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva).
By the word "mind" (manas), however, it is to be inferred that the unmanifest form is the Pradhāna.
In this manner, my Prakṛti—the power known as Māyā—is divided eightfold, having attained distinction;
though it is also divided into twenty-four varieties.
It is said that [the *prakṛti*] is divided into eightfold with the intention of expressing its inclusion within these very eight.
And so, in the chapter on the Field (*kṣetrādhyāya*), he will elaborate upon this very *prakṛti* as consisting of twenty-four principles:
"The great elements, ego-consciousness, intellect, and the unmanifest itself."
"The sense-faculties are eleven, and the objects of the sense-faculties are five. (Gītā 13.5) //4//

Madhusūdana—having thus oriented the listener through this introduction, and demonstrating his own perfection as the Self of all, first presents the lower *prakṛti* in the verse beginning with "Earth" (*bhūmiḥ*).

For according to the Sāṅkhyas, there are eight *prakṛtis*: the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), the Great Principle (*mahat*), and the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). The five [gross elements]...

The five great elements (mahābhūtas), the five organs of action (karmendriyas), the five organs of cognition (jñānendriyas), and the mind (manas) which is common to both— these are called the sixteen transformations (vikāras).
These indeed constitute the twenty-four principles (tattvas).

In that context, the terms "earth," "water," "fire," "air," and "space" indicate the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*)— consisting of smell, taste, form, touch, and sound— which are the subtle states of the five gross elements known as earth, water, fire, air, and space. The terms "intellect" (*buddhi*) and "ego" (*ahaṅkāra*), however, refer to their own primary meanings.

By the word "mind" (manas), the remaining unmanifest (avyakta) is indicated through its grammatical coordination with the word "primordial nature" (prakṛti), since it is necessary to abandon its own primary meaning [in this context]. Alternatively, by the word "mind," its own cause, the ego (ahaṅkāra), is indicated due to its proximity to the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
However, the word "intellect" (buddhi) has its primary application precisely to the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva), which is the cause of the ego.

And by the word *ahaṅkāra*, the unmanifest (*avyakta*)—which consists of ignorance and is permeated by all latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is indicated, because it possesses uncommon attributes such as being the initiator [of the evolution]. In the manner thus described, this immediate Nature (*prakṛti*), known as Māyā, the supreme power of the Lord, whose nature is indefinable, which consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is divided eightfold; that is, it has come to differentiation through eight modes.
The meaning is that the entire category of insentient things is included within this very [category].
Furthermore, in our own established doctrine, the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) are indeed transformations of *māyā* consisting of vision and volition;
and we have stated more than once that the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are the five great elements in their unquintuplicated state. //4//

Viśvanātha: Now, for one possessed of devotion, "knowledge" (jñāna) means precisely the knowledge of the Lord’s sovereignty, and not merely the knowledge of the self as distinct from the body and so forth.

Therefore, while defining the knowledge of His own sovereignty, He speaks of His two-fold nature through the distinction of the higher and the lower in the two verses beginning with "The earth... (14.3–4).
By the words "earth" and so forth, the five gross elements are included together with their subtle counterparts, smell and the rest;
by the word "egoity" (ahaṃkāra), both the sense organs—which are its effects—and the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), which is its cause, are grasped;
the separate mention of intellect (buddhi) and mind (manas) is because of their preeminence among the principles. //4//

Baladeva: Having thus directed the listener, Arjuna, toward Himself, [the Lord] speaks of His two powers—consisting of the conscious and unconscious energies that constitute His causal nature—in the two verses beginning with "The earth... (Gītā 7.4–5).

Primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is twenty-four-fold, is divided eightfold as the essence of the earth and the other elements; it should be understood as "mine" (*madīyā*). Since the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the rest are included within the earth and the other gross elements, they should also be understood here as being twenty-four-fold.
Among those, within the five gross elements beginning with earth, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—which are the causes of smell and the other qualities—are included.
The word "intellect" (buddhi) denotes the principle of the Great (mahat-tattva), which is the ego (ahaṅkāra) along with its eleven effects, the sense organs.
The word "mind" (manas), however, refers to the Pradhāna, whose nature is unmanifest and which is to be apprehended by the mind.
And the Śruti says likewise: "Among those numbered at twenty-four, the unmanifest is called the manifest.
And he himself will state this in the chapter on the Field (Kṣetrādhyāya) beginning with, "The great elements, the ego... [Gītā 13.5]. //4//
But know, O mighty-armed one, that there is another, higher nature of Mine, distinct from this, which is the life-force by which this world is sustained. (7.5)
Śrīdhara: Concluding this lower nature (prakṛti), He speaks of the higher nature with the words "This other...

This eightfold nature that has been described is "lower" because it is inferior due to its insentience and because it exists for the sake of another. From this [nature], know—that is, understand—My other nature, which is distinct, superior, and of the nature of the individual soul (jīva).
The cause of its being "other" is that consciousness, which takes the form of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), by means of its own karma, sustains this world. //5//

Madhusūdana: Thus, while describing the inferiority of *prakṛti* characterized as the field (*kṣetra*), He speaks of the supreme *prakṛti* characterized as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) with the words "This other...

(*apareyam*). That *prakṛti* which was previously described as eightfold and consists of the entire class of insentient things—this is the "other" (*aparā*), meaning inferior, because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*), because it exists for the sake of another (*parārthatva*), and because it takes the form of bondage to *saṃsāra*.
But from this *prakṛti* characterized as the field—which consists of the class of insentient things—[He speaks of] another, indeed distinct [from it], indicated by the word "but" (*tu*).

Know, O mighty-armed one, that my supreme, pure, and excellent nature— which is of the character of the individual soul (jīva), conscious in essence, characterized as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), and incapable of being differentiated from Me in any way—
is that by which this world, consisting of insentient matter, has been entered within through that nature characterized as the individual soul.
It is supported by itself, yet it is held up by this living self (jīva), according to the Śruti: "Having entered [it] with this living self, let me manifest name and form.
The intention is that it is not possible to support [the world] devoid of the living self. //5//
Viśvanātha: This *prakṛti*, known as *variyaṅga* (the inferior limb), is an *aparā* (lower) power because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*).
Know that the *prakṛti* other than this—the *taṭasthā* (intermediate) power, which is the *jīva* (individual soul)—is *parā* (higher) because of its sentience (*caitanyatva*).
The reason for its superiority is that by means of this consciousness (*cetanā*), this insentient world is grasped for the sake of its own experience. //5//

Baladeva: This is the lower nature (prakṛti), inferior because it is insentient and an object of enjoyment; know that there is another, higher nature than this insentient prakṛti—my own nature, which is the individual soul (jīva-bhūta), superior because it is sentient and the enjoyer. O mighty-armed Pārtha!
The reason for this otherness is expressed by the word "yayā" (by which).
By which consciousness this world is sustained through its own karma and is grasped for its own enjoyment, like a bed or a seat;
and scripture declares that this power belongs to Hari alone, saying of You: "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16).
Understand that all beings have this as their source; I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe. (7.6)

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating that these two are the material causes (prakṛti), He declares His own status as the cause of creation and so forth through them with the words "these" (etad). These two, consisting of the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), are the "sources" (yoni)—that is, the causal grounds—of which [all things] are composed; such are "those whose source is these" (etad-yonīni).
Understand, that is, realize, that all beings consist of the stationary and the moving.
In this regard, the insentient *prakṛti* transforms into the form of the body,
while the sentient [aspect], which is a portion of Me, enters into bodies as the experiencer and sustains them through its own karma;
and both these *prakṛtis* of Mine have originated from Me.

Therefore, I alone am the source (*prabhava*) of the entire world together with its material nature (*saprakṛtika*). "Source" means that from which [the world] pre-eminently (*prakarsena*) comes into being;
the meaning is that I am the supreme cause.
Likewise, "pralaya" means that by which [all things] are dissolved;
the meaning is that I alone am also the destroyer. //6//

Madhusūdana: Establishing through inference—based on the mark of effects—that He is the cause of the creation and so forth of the universe by means of those two natures previously described, [the Lord] shows His own causality therein with the words "these have that as their source" (*etad-yonīni*).

These two natures characterized as *kṣetra* (the field) and *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), which were previously mentioned as the lower and the higher, are the "source" (*yoni*) of those things; thus, "those having that as their source" refers to all beings (*bhūtāni*)—all things subject to becoming, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, and possessing birth.

"Understand all things to be thus"—that is, know them as such; since effects consist of the knot of the conscious (cit) and the unconscious (acit), one must infer that the cause also consists of the knot of the conscious and the unconscious.
Thus, since the two *prakṛtis*, characterized as the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), serve as my limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), I [am defined] through them.

The Omniscient One, the Lord of All, whose limiting adjunct is infinite power and *māyā*, is the source— the cause of origination— and likewise the dissolution— the cause of destruction— of the entire world consisting of the moving and the unmoving, of every category of effects; for this illusory manifold, like a dream, He is both the substratum and the object of *māyā*.
The meaning is that I alone am both the illusion and the substrate, as well as the seer. //6//
Viśvanātha: By means of these two powers alone, He declares His own causality of the universe with the word "this" (*etad*).

Know that those beings consisting of the stationary and the moving have as their womb—that is, their cause—these two powers, namely *māyā-śakti* and *jīva-śakti*, which take the form of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Therefore, since the origin of this entire universe is from my two powers, I alone am the creator.
Because that dissolution occurs within me alone, who possess that power, I myself am its destroyer. //6//
Baladeva: By means of these two powers alone, He declares His own causality of the entire universe with the word "this" (etat).
Understand and know that all beings, both moving and stationary, have this as their source (etad-yoni).

The meaning is: those whose sources—meaning causes—are these two powers of Mine, which are designated by the terms *kṣetra* (the field) and *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), and which are respectively lower and higher.
And those two natures are produced from me alone;
therefore, I alone am the source— the cause of origination— of the entire world together with its two natures,
according to the etymological derivation that "it originates from this."
I alone am also the destroyer of that dissolution, according to the etymological derivation: "that by which one is dissolved. //6//
O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Me;
all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. (7)

Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore [it is said] "from Me. From My presence, there is nothing whatsoever that is more supreme—that is, better—than I, being the independent cause of the creation and destruction of the universe. Furthermore, He says "in Me" to indicate that I alone am the cause of its maintenance.
"In me all this world is woven, strung, and supported"—this is the meaning.
The illustration is clear. //7//

Madhusūdana: Since I alone, through *māyā*, am the cause of the birth, sustenance, and destruction of the entire universe, therefore [the world arises] from me in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

From me—who am the substratum of *māyā* transformed into the form of the entirety of the visible world, who illumine everything, and who am the essence of self-luminous supreme bliss-consciousness pervading all as existence and manifestation—[arises the world], just as for one seeing a dream, from that which is ultimately real.

Like a dream-object, like a magical creation of a magician, or like silver imagined by ignorance upon the consciousness delimited by a fragment of mother-of-pearl—there is nothing else whatsoever that is more supreme or ultimately real, O Dhanañjaya.

The meaning is that what is imagined in Me does not, in ultimate reality, differ from Me; for this is the principle established by the Sūtra: "Its non-difference [from the cause is known] from such scriptural indications as the word 'origin' (ārambhaṇa-śabda)" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.14).

From the perspective of conventional experience (*vyavahāra*), however, all this collection of insentient things is woven and strung upon me—who am of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) and of the nature of manifestation (*sphuraṇa-rūpa*). By my existence, it appears as if existent; by my manifestation, it appears as if manifesting. Thus, for the sake of conventional experience characterized by *māyā*, it is rendered fit.
This is merely because everything is strung together by consciousness (*caitanya*).
The illustration is "like clusters of jewels in a thread" (*sūtre maṇi-gaṇā iva*).

Alternatively, the illustration should be explained in its entirety as follows: "like clusters of jewels strung upon a dreamer within the golden womb (*hiraṇyagarbha*), who is the luminous self (*taijasātman*) in the state of dreaming.

Others, however, explain this verse as a rebuttal to the prima facie argument (*pūrva-pakṣa*) stated in the sūtra: "On account of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction" (VS 3.2.31).

Other than Me—the omniscient, the omnipotent, the cause of all—there is no other cause that is higher or more praiseworthy, nor any independent cause for the creation and dissolution of the entire universe, O Dhanañjaya.

Since this is so, therefore, in Me, the cause of all, this entire aggregate of effects is strung together and woven, and not otherwise; as in the case of a collection of jewels on a thread. However, the illustration [of the thread] applies only to the state of being strung together, and not to the status of being the [independent] cause.
"But 'like earrings and so forth in gold' is the appropriate example. //7//
Viśvanātha: Since this is so, he says, "I alone am everything," for there is nothing whatsoever other than me.
This is because of the identity of cause and effect, and because of the identity of power and the possessor of power.
And thus says the Śruti: "Brahman is indeed one, without a second."
"There is no diversity whatsoever here.
Having thus stated that He Himself is the self of all, He declares His state as the inner controller of all with the word "in Me":

this entire world, consisting of both the conscious and the insentient, is of My nature because it is My effect; furthermore, it is strung together and woven within Me, the inner controller, just as clusters of jewels are strung upon a thread.

The venerable Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, however, says that in the aphorism the simile "like a collection of jewels" refers merely to the state of being strung together, and not to causality; rather, "like earrings and so forth in gold" is the appropriate simile. //7//

Baladeva said: "Indeed, although it has been stated that you alone are the possessor of power and the source even for the two natures—the stable and the moving, which are mutually dependent—thereby your status as the seed of the entire universe is understood, yet not your supremacy over all.
And that [seedhood] belongs to someone other than you, distinct from that seed."
That which is higher than that is formless and free from affliction;
those who know this become immortal, while others go only to suffering.
If it be argued that this is because of the scriptural statement [ŚvetU 3.10], he replies to that with the words "from me" (*mattaḥ*).
The meaning is: "From me, Kṛṣṇa, your friend, there is nothing else whatsoever more supreme or better; I alone am the most excellent reality.
Now, if it be objected that this contradicts other scriptural passages such as "that which is higher than that," we say that this objection is weak, for it cannot withstand scrutiny. To explain:
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent as the sun, beyond darkness;
knowing him alone, one becomes immortal in this very world.
"There is no other path for the attainment of the goal," thus [it is said].

The Śvetāśvataras have taught that knowledge of Viṣṇu, the Great Person who is the seed of the entire world, is the path to immortality, and that there is nothing beyond it; and to establish this, they state:
"There is nothing whatsoever higher than which there is another."
Since there is nothing smaller or greater than that, its status as the supreme has been established, along with the impossibility of such a quality in anything other than it;
thereafter, by the passage beginning with "that which is higher and higher," what was previously stated is indeed concluded.
But it has been stated that there is nothing superior to that;
for if that were not the case, it would follow that those [scriptures] are false.
Thus the author of the Sūtra says: "Because of the negation of others" (Vs 3.2.36).
Since there is no one else besides Me who possesses supremacy, He says "in Me" (mayi) to show that I alone am the support of all things other than Myself.
The rest is clearly woven or strung together.
By this, His own role as the protector of the universe is stated. //7//

I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun; I am the sacred syllable *praṇava* in all the Vedas; I am the sound in space; and I am the virility in men. (7.8)
Śrīdhara: He elaborates on His being the cause of the world's maintenance through five verses beginning with "I am the taste.
In the waters, I am the taste; the meaning is that by my manifestation (*vibhūti*) in the form of the subtle element of taste, I abide in the waters by being their substratum.
Likewise, I am the radiance in the moon and the sun.

The meaning is that I abide as the substratum of the moon and the sun by way of my manifestation in the form of light. This should be understood in the same way for what follows. Among all the Vedas, which consist of articulated speech (*vaikharī*), I am the *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*, which is their fundamental source.
In the sky, I am sound in its subtle state;
among men, I am manly effort, for it is in effort that men abide. //8//

Madhusūdana says: One should not doubt how all this is strung upon You, given that it is perceived as being strung upon the tastes and other qualities; for He states in five verses beginning with "I am the taste" that He Himself exists in the form of taste and the rest.

"Taste" refers to the holy, sweet essence, which is the subtle element (*tanmātra*) and the fundamental cause (*sāra*) of all waters—that which is inherent in all waters. O Kaunteya, I am that; in Me, who am of that nature, all waters [are strung].
The meaning is "pervaded.
This same explanation should be applied to all the subsequent sections.
One should not be overly insistent on the idea that this manifestation is taught merely for the purpose of meditation.
Likewise, I am the light of the moon and the sun;
the meaning is that the moon and the sun are woven into me, who am the common nature of light.

Similarly, I am the syllable *oṃ*, which is interwoven through all the Vedas, according to the Vedic revelation: "Just as all leaves are perforated by a stalk, so too is all speech pervaded by the syllable *oṃ*."
"Interwoven" means strung together;
the meaning is that all speech and the entire Veda [are so]. Sound, which is meritorious and consists of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), is "I," pervading the ether (*kha*).
I am the *pauruṣa*, the commonality of being a person (*puruṣatva-sāmānya*), which is woven through all men;
it should be understood everywhere that all particularities are strung upon me, who am the universal form, as illustrated by the Vedic examples of the drum and so forth. //8//

Viśvanātha: He says "I am the essence" in four verses to show that just as I exist here in this world as its effect in the form of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), so too do I exist in some places as the cause, and in others—in human beings and the like—as the essential core (*sāra*). The meaning is: "In water, I am the essence," which is its cause; that is, My own manifestation (*vibhūti*).
Thus it is everywhere, even at the beginning:
*prabhā* is the form of light;
*praṇava* is the syllable *oṃ*, the cause of all the Vedas.
In space, sound is its cause;
among men, human effort—indeed, every specific exertion—is the very essence of humanity. //8//

Baladeva explains the reality [of the Self] through five verses beginning with "I am the essence" (raso 'ham). Among the waters, I am the essence; by means of that subtle element of taste as my manifestation, I abide within them while protecting them, for they cannot exist without it.
In the moon and in the sun, I am the radiance; through that radiance and through my sovereign power, I abide protecting them both.
This should be understood in the same way regarding other things.
Among all the Vedas in their manifest (vaikharī) forms, I am the *praṇava*, which is their fundamental source.
In the sky, I am sound, characterized by its subtle element;
among men, I am manly effort, which bears fruit, for by that alone they remain established. //8//
I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the radiance in the fire; I am the life-force in all beings and the austerity in ascetics. (7.9)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding "meritorious":
"meritorious" refers to the unmodified fragrance, which is the subtle element of fragrance (gandha-tanmātra).
The meaning is that I am the substratum of the earth.

Alternatively, because the state of being a substratum is intended here in the sense of a manifestation (*vibhūti*), and since the fragrant scent is a manifestation by virtue of its excellence, it is called "the holy fragrance.
Likewise, in the fire (*vibhāvasu*), that which is the heat—the innate, unbearable radiance—that am I;
in all beings, that which is life—the wind that sustains the vital breath—that am I; such is the meaning.
Among ascetics, such as forest-dwellers and others, I am the austerity consisting of the endurance of dualities. //9//
Madhusūdana: I am the meritorious, fragrant, and unmodified scent, which is the common form of the entire earth and is called its subtle element (*tanmātra*), pervading the earth.
The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the merit of taste and the other qualities as well.

For sound, touch, form, taste, and scent are meritorious and unmodified by their very nature; it is only due to specific unrighteousness (*adharma*) in living beings that these become non-meritorious, but not by their own nature.
Likewise, that which is the merit in the fire—Vibhāvasu—in the form of the power to burn and illuminate, accompanied by hot touch, and consisting of white, radiant color, that am I.
By the word "and" (ca), it should be understood that the meritorious cool touch in the wind, which refreshes those afflicted by hot touch, that too am I.
Among all beings—all living creatures—I am life, the maintenance of breath, and vitality.
The meaning is that all living beings are woven into Me who am of that nature.

Among ascetics—those constantly engaged in austerity such as forest-dwellers and others—that austerity which consists of the capacity to endure the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and so forth, that I am.
Ascetics are woven into Me who am of that nature, because in the absence of a qualification, there is an absence of the qualified.

By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and austerity" (*tapaś ca*), all forms of austerity are included: both internal austerity, characterized by one-pointedness of mind, and external austerity, characterized by the restraint of the tongue, the generative organ, and so forth. //9//

Viśvanātha: "Punya" refers to pure fragrance; "puṇya" also refers to that which is beautiful, according to Amara. The particle *ca* serves to include the purity of taste and the other [sensory qualities] as well.
"Tejas" (vitality) is the essence consisting of the capacity for digesting all things, illuminating them, providing relief from cold, protection, and so forth.
Life itself is the essence of longevity;
austerity alone—consisting of the endurance of dualities and so forth—is the essence. //9//
Baladeva: "The meritorious, unmodified fragrance characterized by the subtle element (*tanmātra*);
the word 'ca' (and) is intended to include taste and the other qualities as being meritorious as well;

in fire (*vibhāvasu*), the light (*tejas*) consisting of the capacity for cooking all things and illumination; and in air (*śada*), that meritorious touch which removes the distress of those afflicted by hot touch."
This is to be understood as "I.
Life, longevity, austerity, and the endurance of dualities [constitute the self]. //9//
Know Me, O Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid. (7.10)
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, what is the seed?
It is the capacity to produce effects of its own kind, belonging to all beings, both moving and non-moving;
it is eternal, perpetual, and permeates all successive effects.
Know that very seed to be My manifestation;
it does not perish with each individual instance.
Likewise, among the intelligent, I am the intellect—the higher wisdom.
The brilliance of those who are radiant and bold increases their boldness.
Madhusūdana says: If it be argued that all beings are woven upon their respective seeds and not upon You, He says "no," with the word *bījam* (the seed).
Know that which is the one seed—the single cause—of all beings, both stationary and moving;

which is eternal (*sanātana*), constant, independent of any other seed, and not distinct for each individual nor transitory—that unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) seed of all things, know that to be Me alone, and not something separate from Me, O Pārtha.
Therefore, it is logical that all things are woven upon me alone, who am the seed of all; this is the meaning.
Furthermore, I am the intellect (*buddhi*)—the capacity for discriminating between reality and unreality—for those possessed of such intellect.
Those possessing intellect are woven upon me in the form of intellect, because it has been stated that in the absence of a qualifier, there is an absence of the qualified.

Likewise, "splendor" (*tejaḥ*) means boldness, the capacity to overcome others, and "purity" (*pari*) means being invincible; that which belongs to those who possess such splendor—that is, those endowed with such boldness—is what I am.
The meaning is that those who possess splendor are woven into me, whose nature is splendor. //10//
Viśvanātha: "The seed" means the unmodified cause called Pradhāna;
"eternal" means constant; for the wise, intelligence itself is the essence. //10//

Baladeva said: Know that which is the single, eternal, and constant seed of all beings, both moving and unmoving—not distinct for each individual nor transitory—to be none other than Me, known as Pradhāna, the seed of all; by My manifestation in that form, I sustain them, for it is through being intent upon That that they are nourished.
Intelligence (*buddhi*) is that which possesses the discernment between the essential and the non-essential.
Splendor (*tejas*) is boldness, the capacity to overcome others, and the state of being invincible by others. //10//
And I am the strength of the strong, devoid of desire and attachment; O bull among the Bharatas, I am the desire in beings that is not contrary to dharma. 7.11
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, what is *bala*?
*Kāma* is the longing for an object not yet attained; it is *rājasa*.

*Rāga*, on the other hand, is the coloring of the mind (*citta-rañjana*) toward an object already desired, even when that object has been attained, directed toward further objects; it is synonymous with *tṛṣṇā* (thirst) and is *tāmasa*.
I am the strength that is devoid of those two;
the meaning is that I am the sattvic capacity for the performance of one's own duty (sva-dharma).
I am the desire that is not opposed to dharma, which serves solely for the procreation of offspring within one's own wife. //11//

Madhusūdana: Desire (*kāma*) is a specific modification of the mind characterized by the thought, "May this unattained object be attained," even in the absence of the causes for its attainment. Attachment (*rāga*), which consists of passion, is a specific modification of the mind characterized by the thought, "May this attained object not perish," even when there exist causes for its destruction. That [state] which is specifically devoid of these two, being entirely free from them and devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*, is [the state of *nirvikalpa-samādhi*].
That sattvic strength—which is the capacity to sustain the body, senses, and so forth for the performance of one's own duty (svadharma)—belongs to the strong;
that is, it belongs to those possessed of such sattvic strength who have turned their backs on worldly existence (saṃsāra). "I am that" means that the strong are woven into Me in that form.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but), with its position shifted.
The meaning is that power alone, when free from desire and passion, should be meditated upon as being of My nature, and not the power that is the cause of desire and passion for those in saṃsāra.
Alternatively, the word "rāga" may be explained as having the sense of "krodha" (anger).

Dharma is the treatise on righteousness; that desire toward living beings— which is not opposed to, nor prohibited by, that Dharma, or which is even conducive to it— consisting of an inclination directed toward one's wife, children, wealth, and so forth, as permitted by the scriptures,
that am I,
O bull among the Bharatas.
The meaning is that, since I am one whose desires are not opposed to the scriptures, there is delight for those beings who are likewise endowed with such desires. //11//
Viśvanātha: *Kāma* is the desire for one’s own livelihood and so forth; *rāga* is anger. "Free from those" means not arisen from those two.
It is not contrary to the Dharma, being intended solely for the purpose of procreating a son with one's own wife. //11//
Baladeva: *Kāma* is the desire for one's own livelihood and so forth;
*rāga*, however, is the coloring of the mind toward an object already desired, and even further toward something superior to that, which is synonymous with excessive craving (*atitṛṣṇā*).
"Strength devoid of these two" means the capacity to perform one's own duty (*svadharma*).
Not contrary to the Dharma, it is for the sole purpose of procreating a son with one's own wife. //11//

And whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me. 12.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and those which": these are other states of being (bhāva) that are characterized by goodness (sāttvika), such as tranquility (śama), self-control (dama), and so forth;
and those characterized by passion (rājasa), such as exhilaration (harṣa), arrogance (darpa), and so forth.
And the qualities of darkness (tāmasa), such as grief, delusion, and so forth,
arise for living beings through the power of their own karma; know that these are born from Me alone,
because they are the effects of the qualities of My own nature (prakṛti).
Even so, I do not abide in them;
the meaning is that I am not dependent upon them as a living being is. Rather, the meaning is that they, being dependent on me, abide in me. //12//
Madhusūdana: What is the use of such an enumeration with the words "and whatever else"?
Whatever other states there may be that are transformations of the mind—those which are *sāttvika*, such as tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth;
and those which are *rājasa*, such as joy (*harṣa*), pride (*darpa*), and so forth.

Furthermore, understand that all those states of darkness (*tāmasa*)—such as grief, delusion, and so forth—which arise in living beings due to the power of ignorance, karma, and the like, are born from Me alone; know this in the manner previously stated, "I am the source of the entire universe," and so on.

Alternatively, all insentient categories (*jaḍa-varga*), whether characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*), passion (*rājasa*), or darkness (*tāmasa*), may be explained [as being born from Me], as there is no reason for distinction.
The particle *eva* (indeed) has the sense of a comprehensive restriction (*samasta-avadhāraṇa*).

Even so, I am not "in them"; although born from them, even while being colored by their modifications and under their control—just as a piece of rope is colored by all the various forms imagined upon it—I do not become a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*) like those who are subject to worldly existence.
But those entities are imagined within me, like a snake and so forth upon a rope; their existence and manifestation are dependent on me, meaning they are under my control. //12//
Viśvanātha: Thus, certain manifestations (vibhūtis) that constitute the material cause of objects and the essential substance of objects—such as the Rākṣasas and others—have been described.
However, enough with this excessive detail;
He says "And those who... to show that whatever object is dependent upon Me is indeed My manifestation.
Sāttvika states consist of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, as well as the gods and others;
rājasa states consist of joy, pride, and so forth, as well as the asuras and others;
and tāmasa states consist of grief, delusion, and so forth, as well as the rākṣasas and others.
"They arise from Me alone" means they are the effects of the qualities of My own nature;
"I do not abide in them" means that, unlike the individual soul (jīva), I am not subject to them.
But they, remaining subject to me, abide indeed under my authority. //12//
Baladeva: Having thus briefly described some of His manifestations with the words "ye caiva," He speaks of all of them [with the verse beginning] "ye caiva.

Know that all those states—whether characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*) and so forth—which possess mutually distinct natures, and which exist as the bodies, senses, and objects of living beings, as well as their causes, are endowed with their respective powers and have arisen from Me alone.
But I do not abide in them, nor is my existence dependent upon them; rather, they abide in me with their existence dependent upon me—this is the meaning. //12//
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities (guṇas), this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable. (7.13)
Śrīdhara: Why does this world not know You, the Lord who are such as this?
To this he says: "By three.

This world is deluded by these three aforementioned types of states consisting of the *guṇas*—namely, desire, greed, and so forth—which are transformations of the *guṇas* and constitute its very nature.
Therefore, he does not recognize me;
in what way?
As being beyond these entities.
It is untouched by these [qualities] and is their controller;
therefore, it is "immutable," meaning free from modification. //13//

Madhusūdana: Since you, the Supreme Lord, possess absolute sovereignty and a nature that is eternally pure, enlightened, and free from all affliction, how can there be transmigratory existence for the world, which is of your own essence?
If it is argued that this is due to the lack of realization of my true nature as such, then [the author] says "by three" to explain why that very lack of realization exists.

By all these aforementioned threefold states consisting of the qualities— namely, the transformations of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— which possess the nature of becoming, this entire world, the multitude of living beings, has been deluded and rendered incapable of discrimination; yet there exists that which is beyond these states composed of the qualities, the substratum of their conceptualization, and absolutely distinct from them.

The Blessed One shows his compassion, saying: "Alas, what a misfortune for the undiscriminating person! Though I am imperishable, devoid of all modification, free from conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca*), a mass of bliss, self-luminous, and unobstructed, he does not recognize me. Consequently, due to this lack of acquaintance with his own true nature, he wanders as if in saṃsāra. (13)

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "But how is it that these people do not know You, the Supreme Lord, who are of such a nature? To this he says, "By three... (verse 13). The world—the multitude of living beings born within the universe—is deluded by states consisting of the *guṇas*, such as tranquility and self-restraint, or joy, grief, and so forth, which have become its very nature. Because I am devoid of *guṇas*, I am beyond these, imperishable, and changeless.

Baladeva: Now, demonstrating His own nature as the object of meditation, which is distinct from the two powers (śaktis), He states with three verses that attachment to those [powers] is the very cause of ignorance regarding Him:

"by these aforementioned threefold states consisting of the qualities, which are the effects of the qualities of My Māyā, characterized by existence, subject to momentary transformation, and established in the form of bodies, senses, and objects according to their respective past actions."

Deluded— that is, led into a state of lack of discrimination— this entire world, including the multitude of living beings existing as gods, demons, humans, and so forth, does not recognize Me, Kṛṣṇa: the Lord of all, the imperishable one whose nature never declines, the mine of jewels of infinite auspicious qualities, a mass of pure consciousness and bliss, who am beyond and untouched by these states such as the *sāttvika* and others.
He shows resentment toward [him]. //13//
For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the three qualities, is difficult to overcome.
But those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion. (7.14)
Śrīdhara: Who, then, knows you?
To this he says: "Divine" (daivī). Divine means supramundane (alaukikī).
The meaning is "most wonderful.
Consisting of the qualities (*guṇamayī*), that is, having the nature of transformations of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest;
my power, which is Māyā, the Supreme Lord's, is indeed difficult to overcome, that is, hard to cross.
Although this is well known, nevertheless, those who take refuge in me alone—meaning they worship me with unswerving devotion—even they cross over this most difficult-to-traverse illusion;
the sense is that they thereby come to know me. //14//
Madhusūdana: Now, one might raise this objection: since the world is bound by the three qualities of beginningless, established *māyā* as previously described, it lacks independence;

and because it lacks the capacity to abandon those qualities, there can never be a transcendence of *māyā*, for the cause—the incapacity to discern reality—is eternal. Anticipating this, [the author] states that transcendence of *māyā* occurs through taking exclusive refuge in the Blessed Lord, by means of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*).

He says "divine" (daivī) because it is possible [for it to exist there]. It is imagined as being supported by and having as its object that divine one— who is self-luminous, whose nature is self-manifesting consciousness-bliss, who is undivided, and who is established by such scriptural passages as "The divine One God is hidden in all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
For it has been stated: "The indivisible consciousness alone is the possessor of both the state of being the substratum and the state of being the object" (Saṃ. Śārī. 1.319).
This [consciousness] cannot be denied, as it is directly perceived by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*);
furthermore, because of the word "hi" (for/indeed), it is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) since it is the material cause of error.
Consisting of the qualities— that is, having the nature of the three qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—
it is the cause of bondage through its extreme firmness, like a rope made of the three qualities belonging to me,
the illusory Magician, the Supreme Lord, the cause of the entire universe.

Māyā is the inherent nature of the Omniscient and Omnipotent One, which, by virtue of its dependence on Him, brings about the creation and so forth of the universe. It is ignorance (*avidyā*) possessing two powers—obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*)—which is the cause of the appearance of the unreal through the obstruction of the appearance of reality; it is the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) of the entire phenomenal world, according to the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10).
In this regard, the process is as follows:

within consciousness, which is devoid of the distinctions between the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and the world, there is beginningless ignorance (avidyā) superimposed. Being dominated by the quality of sattva, it is clear like a mirror and grasps the reflection of consciousness (cid-ābhāsa), just as a mirror grasps the appearance of a face.

Consequently, the Supreme Lord (parameśvara), who occupies the position of the original object (bimba), is untouched by the defects of the limiting adjunct (upādhi); and the individual soul (jīva), occupying the position of the reflected image (pratibimba), is touched by the defects of the limiting adjunct.

From the Lord, for the sake of the individual soul's experience, there arises the conception that the aggregate of the body and senses, as well as the entire phenomenal world to be experienced by it, is produced through the sequence beginning with space (*ākāśa*).

Just as a face reflected in a mirror follows the original face, consciousness conditioned by the limiting adjunct of *māyā* is conceived as the Witness (*sākṣin*), which conforms to both the Lord and the individual soul.
By that very [Witness], *māyā*—which is superposed upon itself—and its entire effect are illuminated.
Therefore, with reference to the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), the Blessed One said "divine" (daivī), but with reference to the Lord of the image (bimbeśvara), He said "mine" (mama).

Although the individual soul (jīva) is indeed one as the reflection in ignorance (avidyā-pratibimba), nevertheless, because the impressions (saṃskāra) of the internal organs (antaḥ-karaṇa) residing in ignorance are distinct, there is a designation of difference for that [soul] here due to the distinction of its limiting adjunct (upādhi), namely the internal organ—as in the statements: "Those who take refuge in Me alone," and "The wicked and deluded do not take refuge."

The passage beginning with "Four kinds of people worship Me" (Gītā 7.16) and so forth, as well as in the Śruti: "Among the gods, he who awakened to that became that very thing; likewise among the ṛṣis, and likewise among human beings" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10), and so forth—these refer to the individual soul (jīva).

However, when one does not take into account the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), there is a designation here solely in terms of oneness, because the limiting adjunct that constitutes the condition for being a jīva is one and the same.
"Know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields" (Gītā 13.2); "Know both material nature and the person to be indeed beginningless" (Gītā 13.19);
"An eternal fragment of My own self becomes the individual soul in the world of living beings" (Gītā 15.7), and so forth.
And in the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman,' and therefore it became all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10);
"The one God is hidden in all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11);
"Having entered by means of this living self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

If the tip of a hair is divided into a hundred parts, and each part is further divided into a hundred, the living being (jīva) should be known as one such part; yet it is capable of becoming infinite.
[Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9] and so forth.

Although the reflection of Caitra in a mirror does not know itself or another because it is only the insentient aspect that is reflected therein, nevertheless, the reflection of consciousness knows both itself and another precisely because it is consciousness.

In the view that it is a reflection (*pratibimba*), since the mere presence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) within the consciousness of the original object (*bimba*) is imagined; and in the view that it is a manifestation (*ābhāsa*), although that manifestation is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), it is nonetheless distinct from the insentient.

And as long as it does not know its own identity with its original object, it experiences thousands of modifications residing in the limiting adjunct—such as trembling and so forth—as the sun reflected in water [experiences] the tremors of the water.
This is what is meant by the term "difficult to transcend" (*duratyayā*).
It is difficult to transcend—that is, impossible to cross over—without the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of identity with the Lord who is the prototype (*bimba*).

For this very reason, the individual soul (*jīva*), being delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), perceives only that which is connected to it through the doors of the eyes and other senses, and thus becomes a knower of only a little (*kiñcijjña*).
Consequently, the thought "I know," "I act," and "I enjoy" becomes a vessel for hundreds of calamities.

However, if one constantly propitiates the Blessed One— who is like a mirror-image, possessed of infinite power, the controller of *māyā*, the all-knowing, the giver of all fruits, whose form is a mass of bliss, and who manifests numerous incarnations to grace his devotees— by means of total self-surrender (*samarpaṇa*), then, because that which is surrendered to the original image reflects back upon the reflection, one attains all the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*).
Intending this very point, Prahlāda said: "This Lord, who is full of His own self-sufficiency, does not accept honor from ignorant people out of compassion."
"Whatever honor people offer to the Blessed One,
that is for their own sake, just as the beauty of a face is reflected in its reflection.
Thus, if the beauty of the tilaka and other ornaments on a face reflected in a mirror is desired, it must be applied to the original face itself.
She herself reflects there; there is no other means whatsoever for its attainment.

Just so, the individual soul (jīva), which is like a reflection, attains that [Self] only when it is surrendered to the Lord, who is the original object (bimba); there is no other means for the soul to obtain its supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). This is the meaning of the analogy and the thing illustrated.

When his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), through his continuous worship of the Infinite Lord, becomes free from the sin that obstructs knowledge and is augmented by merit conducive to knowledge, then— just as a face appears in an extremely pure mirror-surface— in that exceedingly clear internal organ, [the Self is revealed] by means of the renunciation of all actions, tranquility, self-control, and so forth, preceded by approaching a teacher, hearing the Vedāntic texts, reflecting upon them, and meditating on them.

In the Sanskrit language, there arises a cognitive modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of direct realization— having the form of consciousness free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi-caitanya*) and devoid of the form of the non-self— which is brought about by the Vedāntic statement "That Thou Art" as taught by the Guru, in the form "I am Brahman.
And the consciousness reflected within that modification immediately uproots the ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in its own object, just as a lamp dispels darkness.
Then, due to its destruction, there follows the destruction of the entire manifold of effects along with that mode of functioning;
for it is an established tenet in all systems (*sarva-tantra-siddhānta*) that the destruction of the material cause entails the destruction of the effect.
The Blessed One said this very thing: "Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion (*māyā*). [The word] *ātman*...
Just as in such scriptural passages as "one should meditate thus" (BAU 1.4.7), "he knew him alone as the Self" (BAU 1.4.10),
"the wise man, having realized him alone" (BAU 4.4.23),
and "having known him alone, one goes beyond death" (ŚvetU 6.15), so too here in the phrase "me alone," the particle *eva* is intended to convey the sense of non-contamination (*anuparaktatā*).

Those who take refuge in Me alone— the undivided Self that is pure Consciousness, devoid of all adjuncts, and whose nature is knowledge, bliss, and eternity— by means of a mental modification (*ceto-vṛtti*) produced by the ripening of *nididhyāsana*, which is the fruit of all good deeds, characterized by the attribute of being the form of pure Consciousness beyond verbal description, consisting of non-conceptual direct realization (*nirvikalpa-sākṣātkāra*) born from the statements of the Vedānta, and which is antagonistic to all ignorance and its effects; [they attain liberation].

Those who take this as their object—whoever they may be—cross over and transcend this illusion, which is so difficult to overcome and the source of all misfortune, with effortless ease. Regarding them, the Śruti declares: "Neither the gods nor others have power over his failure, for he becomes the Self of these" (BAU 1.4.10).
The meaning is that they remain as the very essence of the solid mass of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānandaghana) through the cessation of the ocean of transmigratory existence.
The use of the plural number is for the purpose of restating the delusion of the multiplicity of selves, which is based upon the distinctions within the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth.
Where "they behold" (*prapaśyanti*) ought to be said, the expression "they attain" (*prapadyante*) has been used; thus, being my sole refuge, they attain me alone—
the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— who is the very essence of infinite beauty, the abode of the entire collection of all arts, whose pair of lotus feet possess a splendor exceeding that of a fresh lotus,
whose mind is ever intent on playing in Vṛndāvana while engaged in the constant sounding of the flute, and who sportively lifted the mountain named Govardhana.

Those whose minds are submerged in the great ocean of the bliss of my love spend their days incessantly meditating upon Gopāla—the destroyer of the host of wicked ones such as Śiśupāla and Kaṃsa; whose feet possess the entirety of the splendor of fresh rain-clouds; whose form consists of the very essence of supreme bliss; and who embodies the entire manifestation of Brahmā. Thus, they are not overcome by any of the transformations of the qualities of Māyā.

However, fearing that these [sages], who are skilled in the pleasures of my own amorous play, might be capable of uprooting me, Māyā withdraws from them— just as a courtesan flees from wrathful ascetics.
Therefore, it is also the intention of the Blessed One that one seeking to cross over Māyā should constantly meditate upon Me in this very way.
In this matter, the Śrutis and Smṛtis are to be accepted as authoritative. //14//
Viśvanātha: [Objection: "In that case, how do they transcend the delusion consisting of the three *guṇas*? To this he says: "Divine" (*daivī*).
The meaning is: "divine" refers to those who sport (*dīvyanti*) with the bliss of sense objects, namely the *jīvas*; it is the deluder of them.
Consisting of the *guṇas*, through their cohesion, it takes the form of a great noose with three coils.
This *māyā* of mine, the Supreme Lord, is my external power (*bahiraṅga-śakti*), which is difficult to overcome and impossible to transcend.
In the context of the "noose," the meaning is that it cannot be cut or untied by anyone.
"But have faith in my words," saying this, he touched his own chest and said to me, "I am indeed of a dark and beautiful form. (14)

Baladeva: If it be objected that because the *māyā* consisting of the three *guṇas* is eternal, the cessation of delusion caused by it is difficult to achieve, [the Lord] says "daivī" (divine) in response.
This *māyā* of Mine, the Lord of all, the inconceivable and most wonderful creator of the infinite universe, is "divine";
the meaning is that it is supramundane and exceedingly marvelous.
It is such because it serves as the instrument for the creation of the universe;
and the Śruti says likewise: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10), and so forth.
It is composed of the Guṇas, meaning its nature consists of the three Guṇas, beginning with Sattva.
By way of wordplay (*śleṣa*), it is like a rope tripled [into three strands], which, due to its extreme firmness, is the cause of bondage for living beings;
therefore, it is "difficult to cross" (*duratyayā*) for them, meaning it is difficult to overcome.
In the case of the rope, the sense is that they are unable to cut it or untie it.
Even though it is thus, he says "Me" to show that its cessation may occur through devotion to Me: those who, by virtue of such association with the virtuous,

take refuge in Me— Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all, the controller of Māyā, and an ocean of affection for those surrendered to Him— they cross over this Māyā, which is as boundless as the ocean, with ease, as if crossing a mere handful of water from a cow's hoofprint.

"Having crossed that [ocean] which has but a single flavor, they reach me, their own Lord, who am inclined toward grace. By the word "me alone," the particle "eva" (alone) indicates that crossing it by means of *prapatti* (surrender) through others than me—such as Brahmā, Rudra, and so forth—is not possible; and the Śruti says this very thing in passages such as "Only by knowing Him... and so on, as well as the gods said to Mucukunda:
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—with the sole exception of *kaivalya* (liberation) from us today;
for there is but one Lord, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the imperishable.
Thus spoke Śiva to Ghaṇṭākarṇa: "Viṣṇu alone is the bestower of liberation for all; of this there is no doubt. (14)
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in Me; their wisdom carried away by illusion, they have resorted to a demonic nature. (7.15)
Śrīdhara: If this is so, then why do all people not worship you alone?
To this he says: "Not me.
Those among men who are inferior do not approach me; they do not worship me.
The reason for their inferiority is that they are deluded, being devoid of discrimination.
Why is that? Because they are evildoers, characterized by sinful conduct.
Therefore, they are those whose knowledge—even though it has arisen from the instructions of the scriptures and teachers—is stolen away and cast out by illusion (*māyā*).
Therefore, having attained the demoniacal nature and disposition which will be described by the words "hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, and even harshness," they do not worship Me. //15//
Madhusūdana: If this is so, then why do all people not take refuge in you alone—the Blessed One—for the uprooting of *māyā*, which is the root of all misfortune?
[To this] the Blessed One says, "Not me," because they are hindered by long-accumulated evil deeds (*durita*);
that is, they are constantly joined with evil through their sinful actions.
