Therefore, among men, these are the lowest, censurable by the virtuous in this world and partakers of thousands of misfortunes in the next.

Why do the deluded always commit evil deeds which are the very cause of misfortune? Because they are devoid of discrimination, not knowing "this is the means to achieve one's goal" and "this is the means to achieve misfortune. Even when the means of valid knowledge exists, why do they not discriminate? Because their wisdom has been stolen away by *māyā* in the form of the delusion of identity with the aggregate of the body and the senses.
Those whose knowledge—the capacity for discernment (*viveka*)—has been stolen away or obstructed by the aforementioned transformed *māyā* are such [as described].

Therefore, having resorted to the demonic nature (*āsura-bhāva*) characterized by violence, falsehood, and so forth—which will be described later in the passage beginning with "Hypocrisy, arrogance, and self-conceit, as well as anger and harshness" (Gītā 16.4)—they are unfit for the realization of Me; thus, they do not take refuge in Me, the Lord of All, nor do they worship Me.
The intended meaning is: "Alas, what misfortune is theirs! //15//
Viśvanātha: [Objection] But then, why is it that even some scholars do not take refuge in you? [Response] Those who are truly wise indeed take refuge in me;
it is only those who merely imagine themselves to be wise who do not take refuge in me—this is what he says with the words "not me."
Those who are evil-doers and wicked, yet consider themselves skillful and wise, are "badly wise"—this is the meaning.
They are of four kinds:
some are deluded, like beasts, though they perform ritual actions. As it has been said:
"Surely those who, struck down by fate, abandon the nectar of the stories of Acyuta to listen to the tales of the wicked—just as excrement-eaters consume feces—are truly ruined. And:
"Who indeed, other than a non-human being, would not serve Mukunda?"

Others, the lowest of men, though they have attained human birth through devotion for some time, think at the end that the means of practice are of no use for attaining the fruit; thus, abandoning devotion of their own accord, their very inferiority is characterized by this self-inflicted abandonment of devotion—this is the sense.

Others, despite being engaged in teaching the scriptures and so forth, have their knowledge stolen away by *māyā*; for them, the form of Nārāyaṇa, which shines in Vaikuṇṭha, is the one to be reached through constant devotion.
The meaning is that they do not consider the forms of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others to be human; as will be said: "The deluded disregard me when I have assumed a human body" (Gītā 9.11).
The sense is that even though they approach me, they do not truly approach me.
Others have resorted to an asuric nature;
asuras such as Jarāsandha and others, aiming at my physical form, pierce it with arrows.
In the same way, by means of fallacious arguments based on causes such as perceptibility and so forth, they indeed seek to undermine my form, even though it resides in Vaikuṇṭha.
But the meaning is that they do not attain [it]. //15//

Baladeva: [Objection: "If indeed those who have taken refuge in you alone are liberated, then why do some even among the learned (*paṇḍita*) not take refuge in you? To this he says: "Not me" (*na mām*).

Those who are both wicked (*duṣṭa*) and self-satisfied scholars (*kṛtinaḥ*)—that is, those who are skilled in the meaning of the scriptures—are "wicked scholars" (*duṣkṛtinaḥ*); such bad scholars do not take refuge in me.
And the Śruti speaks thus: [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.2]...
Existing in the midst of ignorance,
yet considering themselves wise and learned,
the deluded ones wander about, running hither and thither.
"Just like blind men being led by one who is blind" (KaṭhU 1.2.5).

They are of four kinds: some are deluded by *māyā* and are inert regarding *karma*, who—like Indra and others—regard even me, Viṣṇu, as a subordinate part of *karma* and as dependent on *karma* like an ordinary soul (*jīva*).

Others, the lowest of men, though born into families such as those of Brahmins and thereby attaining the status of the best among men through *māyā*, become base commoners due to their attachment to the false meanings of wicked poetry. As it has been said:

"Surely those who, struck down by destiny, abandon the nectar of the stories of the Infallible One (Acyuta) to listen to the tales of the wicked—just as excrement-eaters [abandon nectar to eat] feces—are surely destroyed by fate.
Thus [it is said]. Others, such as the followers of Sāṅkhya and so forth, have had their knowledge stolen away by Māyā.

For they, while denying me as the Lord— whose omniscience, universal sovereignty, status as the creator of all, and role as the giver of liberation are established by thousands of scriptural texts— instead postulate that primordial nature (prakṛti) alone is the creator of all and the bestower of liberation;
in this regard, the cause for their propounding hundreds of such crooked and fallacious arguments is nothing other than Māyā.
However, some who, through mere illusion, have adopted an asuric disposition and advocate for a consciousness-only (cinmātra) that is devoid of distinctions—

just as asuras pierce my form, which bestows all bliss, with arrows, so too do they, by means of reasons such as "unperceivability," attempt to refute that [Self] which is well-known in the Śrutis as being the eternally conscious Self; therefore, in that regard as well, one must produce a corresponding realization.
Illusion itself is the cause. //15//
O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom. (7.16)
Śrīdhara: But those of virtuous deeds indeed worship me;
they are of four kinds according to the gradation of their merit, as he says with the words "of four kinds. Those who have performed meritorious acts in previous births worship me.
They are of four kinds.
The afflicted person is one who is overwhelmed by intense impulses and the like; if he has previously performed meritorious deeds, then he resorts to me.
Otherwise, by resorting to inferior deities, he wanders in saṃsāra.
The same should be understood for what follows hereafter.
"One who desires to know" (jijñāsu) is one who seeks knowledge of the self.
"One who seeks wealth" (arthārthin) is one who desires wealth as a means for enjoyment, whether in this world or the next.
And the man of knowledge is one who knows the Self. //16//

Madhusūdana: Those who are free from demonic tendencies, possess virtuous deeds, and are discriminative, being of four types according to the degree of their meritorious actions, worship Me; and through My grace, they gradually cross over Māyā by becoming devoid of desire—this He declares with the words "of four types."
Those people who are doers of good deeds, having accumulated a store of merit in previous births, are those whose lives have borne fruit; they alone, and no others, worship and serve me.
O Arjuna, these are of four kinds: three of them possess desires, while one is free from desire.
One who is afflicted by suffering— seized by calamities such as enemies, disease, and so forth— and desiring the cessation thereof;
just as the people dwelling in Vraja [suffered] when Indra rained because he was angered by the interruption of the sacrifice,
or as the multitude of kings imprisoned in the dungeon of Jarāsaṃdha.
And Draupadī at the gambling hall while her garment was being pulled away;
the lordly elephant seized by a crocodile;
and the seeker who desires self-knowledge and yearns for liberation.
Just as Mucukunda,
or Janaka of Mithilā and Śrutadeva, and as Uddhava when the Mausala-parvan had concluded— [each] being a seeker of the ultimate goal.
Desirous of obtaining those articles of enjoyment which exist either in this world or in the next,
there are examples here such as Sugrīva and Vibhīṣaṇa, and in the next world, such as Upamanyu and Dhruva.
All three of these also cross over *māyā* by means of worshiping the Blessed One.

Among them, the seeker (*jijñāsu*) crosses over *māyā* directly through the arising of knowledge; whereas the distressed (*ārta*) and the seeker of wealth (*arthārthin*) cross it over by attaining the state of a seeker—this is the distinction.

Since the possibility of being a seeker exists for both the distressed and the seeker of wealth, and the possibility of being distressed, possessing the instruments of knowledge, and seeking wealth exists for the seeker, the seeker is mentioned between the two.
Thus, these three types of devotees with desire have been explained; now the fourth, the one without desire—the *jñānī*—is described.
*Jñāna* is the direct realization of the reality of the Lord; one who is eternally united with that is a *jñānī*, having crossed over *māyā* and being free from all desires.
The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include within the category of the *jñānī* any devotee whatsoever who possesses desireless love.
O bull among the Bharatas, the meaning is: "Do not doubt whether you yourself are one who merely desires to know, or one who possesses knowledge, or which type of devotee you are.
In this regard, a disinterested (niṣkāma) devotee who is a knower is like Sanaka and others, like Nārada, like Prahlāda, like Pṛthu, or like Śuka;
whereas a devotee of pure love free from desire is like the Gopīs and others, or like Akrūra, Yudhiṣṭhira, and so forth.
Kaṃsa, Śiśupāla, and others, although they were constantly intent on thinking of the Lord due to fear and hatred, were not devotees because of the absence of attachment to the Lord.

Furthermore, the nature, the means, and the varieties of devotion—which consists of attachment to the Lord—along with the characteristics of those devotees, have been explained by us in detail in the *Bhagavad-bhakti-rasāyana*; therefore, we shall desist here. 16.
Viśvanātha: To the question, "In that case, who are those who worship you? he says, "Of four kinds.
Being endowed with *sukṛta*—that is, the dharma characterized by the conduct of one's caste (*varṇa*) and stage of life (*āśrama*)—they worship me.
Among them, the *ārta* is one seized by calamities such as disease and desiring their cessation.
The seeker of knowledge (*jijñāsu*) is one who desires self-knowledge or the knowledge of sciences such as grammar;
the seeker of wealth (*arthārthī*) is one who desires worldly and otherworldly enjoyments, such as land, elephants, horses, women, gold, and so forth.
These three types of householders are those with desires (*sakāma*).
The wise one with a purified inner organ is the fourth, the renunciant who is free from desire.
Thus, these four primary qualified persons for devotion have been described.
Among them, in the first three, devotion is mixed with ritual action (*karma*).
In the final fourth [chapter], that which is mixed with knowledge is described;
furthermore, in the subsequent text beginning with "having closed all doors" (Gītā 8.12), that which is mixed with yoga will also be taught.

However, that devotion which is unmixed with knowledge, action, and so forth—being purely absolute (kevalā)—is stated at the very commencement of the seventh chapter by the verse: "O Pārtha, with the mind attached to Me" (Gītā 7.1).

Furthermore, in the eighth chapter, by the verse beginning "With mind ever fixed on Me" (Gītā 8.14), in the ninth chapter, by the two verses beginning "But the great-souled ones, O Pārtha... (Gītā 9.13), and by the verse "Thinking of Me with undivided devotion... (Gītā 9.22), this [devotion] is to be defined.
Thus, in this middle hexad of chapters, the Blessed Lord has taught only two kinds of devotion: that which is predominant and that which is exclusive.
As for that third type of devotion which is seen as subordinate (guṇībhūta) toward the knower and the yogi, performed for the sake of attaining the fruits of action and so forth—
it does not receive the designation of "devotion" because it lacks primacy;
rather, in each such case, it is the actions and other factors themselves that hold primacy.

According to the principle that designations are made based on predominance, there are the designations "possessor of action," "possessor of knowledge," and "possessor of yoga"; likewise, for those who possess these qualities, there are the designations "agent," "knower," and "yogi," but not the designation "devotee."

The fruit of action performed with desire is heaven; the fruit of action performed without desire is the yoga of knowledge; and the fruit of the two types of yoga of knowledge is liberation in the form of *nirvāṇa*.
Now, the fruit of the two-fold devotion (*bhakti*) is stated:

among the various forms of devotion, within the three beginning with the distressed (*ārta*), those three which are mixed with action and characterized by desire have as their fruit the attainment of whatever is desired.

Due to the excellence of the object [of worship], at the end of that [practice], there is the attainment of liberation characterized by *sālokya* (residing in the same world), which is preeminent with happiness and sovereignty;
however, there is no falling back, as occurs at the conclusion of the enjoyment of heaven, which is the fruit of ritual action (*karma*).
As it will be said: "Even those who sacrifice to me come to me" (*Gītā* 9.25).
The fruit of the fourth [type of devotion], which is mixed with knowledge (*jñāna*), is a superior state of peaceful delight (*śānta-rati*), as seen in the case of Sanaka and others.
Due to the predominance of the devotee’s compassion for the Lord, the fruit of a certain [type] of that devotion is the excellence of love (*prema*), as seen in the case of Śrī Śuka and others.
If devotion mixed with ritual action (*karma*) is free from desire (*niṣkāma*), then its fruit is devotion mixed with knowledge.
Its fruit has already been stated.

Furthermore, in some cases, even for those possessing devotion mixed with knowledge, ritual action, and so forth, there may arise a love characterized by servitude and the like—either by its very nature or through the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from association with devotees such as servants;
however, this [love] is primarily focused on majesty (*aiśvarya*).

Furthermore, it has been established many times in the *Śrībhāgavata-ṭīkā* that for pure devotion—which is unmixed with knowledge, ritual action, and so forth, and which possesses numerous divisions such as "the peerless," "possessing nothing else," and "supreme"—the fruit is precisely the state of being an attendant (*pārṣada*) characterized by love such as servitude (*dāsya*), friendship (*sakhya*), and the like.
Here too, in accordance with the context, the distinction between the goal of devotion (*sādhya-bhakti*) has been briefly shown. //16//
Baladeva: To the question "Who, then, take refuge in You?", He says: "Fourfold.
People who are virtuous and highly learned—endowed with the performance of duties appropriate to their own caste and stage of life and with exclusive devotion to Me—worship Me;
and they are of four kinds.

Among them, the "afflicted" (ārta) is one seized by calamities such as enemies or mental afflictions (kleśa), desiring their destruction, such as Gajendra and others. The "seeker of knowledge" (jijñāsu) is one desiring knowledge of the nature of the solitary Self, such as Śaunaka and others.
The "seeker of wealth" (arthārthin) is one desiring prosperity such as a kingdom, such as Dhruva and others.
The man of knowledge, such as Śuka and others, has known himself as the subordinate (śeṣa) and Me, the Supreme Self, as the one to whom He is subordinate (śeṣin).
Among these, the distressed and the rest possess desires,
whereas the man of knowledge is free from desire.
Between those two—the afflicted person and the seeker of wealth—for the sake of achieving the desire for knowledge in the next world, the seeker of knowledge is introduced. //16//
Among them, the man of knowledge, who is ever-disciplined and single-mindedly devoted, is preeminent; for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me. (7.17)
Śrīdhara: Among them, the man of knowledge (jñānī) is the best; thus he says, "Among them...
Among them, the man of knowledge is distinguished.
Here are the reasons: he is "ever-united" (nitya-yukta), meaning he is always established in Me.
He is one whose devotion is directed toward Me alone.

Because the knower (jñānin) lacks the conceit of identification with the body and so forth, there is an absence of mental distraction; thus, for him, both constant yoga and exclusive devotion are possible, but not for anyone else.
For this very reason, I am exceedingly dear to him, and he is mine.
Therefore, the meaning is that he is the best because of these four reasons, beginning with being ever-devoted. //17//

Madhusūdana: [Objection: But surely, by the statement "The wicked, the deluded, the lowest of men do not resort to Me," it follows by implication that those of opposite character—the virtuous—do worship Me; and although this is so, their fourfold division was shown by the verse "Four kinds of people worship Me. Therefore, since all of them are equally virtuous without distinction, [the Lord] says the following in response to that:
Although all four types are certain to be doers of good deeds, [the wise one] is distinguished because of his excellence in merit, due to his disinterestedness and abundance of love;

therefore, "from among them" means that among those four types, the *jñānī*—one who possesses knowledge of reality and from whom all desires have ceased—is distinguished, excels in every respect, and is the most excellent.
This is because he is "ever-united" (*nitya-yukta*) with the Lord, whose nature is non-different from the inner self, having a mind always absorbed in Him due to the absence of distractions.
Therefore, "having exclusive devotion" means one whose devotion—meaning attachment—is directed toward the Lord alone; this is because for such a person, there is no other object of attachment.
Indeed, because of that.

The knower is "dear" (priya), meaning he is the object of unconditional love; because I, the Supreme Self non-different from the inner self (pratyag-ātman), am that knower, he is exceedingly dear to me, the Supreme Lord.
The meaning is that it is well known in both the Vedas and the world that the Self is the most beloved of all. //17//
Viśvanātha: In response to the inquiry as to which among the four types of devotees qualified for devotion is the best, he says:
among them, the man of knowledge (jñānī) is distinguished as the most excellent;
he is "ever-united" because he is constantly united with Me.
The meaning is that because his mind has been brought under control through the practice of knowledge, he is one whose mind is single-pointed (*aikāgra-citta*);
the implication is that the three types beginning with the distressed (*ārta*) are not like this.
[Objection: But does not every person of knowledge indeed worship You out of fear that their knowledge would otherwise be rendered useless?

Regarding this, he says: "He for whom devotion is singular"—meaning that it is his primary and principal quality; or rather, he is one whose devotion is truly singular because of its exclusive attachment, such that he is called a "knower" (*jñānin*) by name alone.
For such a knower, I—whose form is Śyāmasundara—are exceedingly dear, being impossible to abandon in both the stages of the means (*sādhana*) and the goal (*sādhya*).
According to the principle stated in [Gītā 4.11], "In whatever way they approach me, even so do I reward them," he too is dear to me. //17//

Baladeva: With the words "of them," he declares the superiority of the man of knowledge among the four. The man of knowledge is distinguished; that is, he becomes the best, because he is ever-steadfast and single-mindedly devoted.

Because he is free from the desire for the destruction of suffering and so forth, the yogin is eternally united with Me. However, as for those who are distressed (ārta) and others, they attain whatever they desire; My yoga consists in being the sole bestower of that which is desired by them. Therefore, the man of knowledge (jñānin) is superior to the distressed and the rest, because his devotion is directed toward Me alone.
Being insatiable, [the Lord] says, "For he is dear."
For the wise one, I am exceedingly dear, being the very locus of love.

Indeed, he is immersed in the ocean of the nectar of my own dearness and perceives nothing else; the word "exceedingly" (atyartha) is used to indicate that his measure of my dearness cannot be fathomed.
The meaning is that even I, who am omniscient and possessed of infinite power, am unable to describe it.
And that wise one is likewise dear to Me, according to the principle stated in Gītā 4.11, "In whatever way they approach Me, in that same way do I favor them.
The meaning is that My own affection for him is similarly limited. //17//
All these are indeed noble; however, the man of knowledge is my very self—that is my conviction—for he, with a disciplined mind, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal. 18.
Śrīdhara: In that case, do the other three transmigrate as his devotees?
"No, certainly not," he says with the word *udārāḥ*.
The meaning is that all these [four] are noble and great, and are indeed partakers of liberation.

But as for the man of knowledge, my considered opinion is that he is indeed the Self itself; for because that man of knowledge, being one whose self is disciplined and whose mind is fixed on Me alone, has resorted to—that is, taken refuge in—Me alone, who am the unsurpassed goal (anuttamāṃ gatim) of which there is nothing higher, meaning he does not regard any other fruit apart from Me. //18//
Madhusūdana: Are those such as the distressed (ārta) not dear to you?
No; he says "noble" (udārāḥ) because of the qualification "exceedingly so.

Even though these—the distressed and the others—possess desires, all three types of My devotees are indeed noble, that is, excellent, because they possess a multitude of merits accumulated over many previous births.
For otherwise, they would not worship me at all;
for it is frequently observed that those who are afflicted, those seeking knowledge, and those desiring wealth, if they turn away from me, often become devotees of minor deities.
Therefore, they are truly dear to me.
Indeed, no devotee—whether possessed of knowledge or ignorant—is ever unloved by Me;
rather, it is established by the very nature of things that whatever kind of love one has for Me, I likewise have that same kind of love for them.
In this regard, for the three types of devotees who possess desires, that which they desire is dear to them, and I too am dear to them.
But for the knower, who is devoid of any other object of affection, I alone am the object of unsurpassed love;
therefore, he too is the object of my unsurpassed love—this is the distinction. Otherwise, I would lack gratitude and would instead be ungrateful.
For this very reason, the qualification "exceedingly" (*atyartham*) was previously employed.

For instance, in the passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*), that alone becomes more powerful," the sense of the suffix *-tara* (comparative) is intended to be expressed; therefore, [the action] performed apart from knowledge and so forth [is implied].
Action indeed becomes powerful as well;

for since it is stated that "one who possesses supreme knowledge and is devoted is dear to Me," it follows by implication that even one who is a devotee apart from [theoretical] knowledge is likewise dear.
This is because the qualification "supremely" (atyartham) is intended to be significant.
For it has been said: "In whatever way people approach Me, in that same way do I reward them" (Gītā 4.11).
Therefore, the one who possesses knowledge is the wise man who knows Me as the Self;
he thinks, "The Self is indeed not different from Me; He is I myself"—this is My conviction.

The word *tu* serves to highlight the distinction of being free from desire (*niṣkāmatva*) and not perceiving duality, in contrast to the triad [of yogīs] who perceive such distinctions while possessing desire.
For (*hi*),

because that knower (*jñānī*), whose self is disciplined (*yuktātmā*)— meaning one whose mind is always absorbed in Me— goes to Me, the Blessed One, the infinite mass of bliss, the Self itself, as the unsurpassed (*anuttamā*), most excellent goal (*gati*) to be reached.
He has resorted to, that is, accepted, the supreme fruit; the meaning is that he does not consider any fruit other than Me to exist. //18//
Viśvanātha: If that is so, are the three types beginning with the distressed (ārta) not dear to you? To this he replies, "No, indeed, no," by saying "the noble ones" (udārāḥ).
The sense is: those who worship me and accept from me whatever they desire—which I myself am eager to give—are truly dear to me, for I am affectionate toward my devotees and a giver of much.
But the man of knowledge is indeed My very Self; for while he worships Me, he does not desire from Me anything such as heaven or liberation.
Therefore, it is My conviction—that is, My firm opinion—that since he is dependent on Me, he is My very Self.
This is because he has attained Me, who am of the form of Śyāmasundara, as his unsurpassed, most excellent goal, and remains fixed in that certainty.
But my intention is not that there is liberation as Brahman, whose nature is devoid of distinctions.
And thus, the wise devotee who possesses devotion characterized primarily by freedom from desire is regarded by the Lord—who is affectionate toward His devotees—as His very own self;
whereas the exclusive devotee (*ananya*) is regarded with even greater esteem than the self. As it has been said:
"Neither my own source (Brahmā), nor Śaṅkara, nor Saṅkarṣaṇa, nor Śrī, nor even my own self is as dear to me as you are. And:
"I do not desire myself without the virtuous devotees of mine."
"Though delighting in the Self, he took delight [in her]," and so forth. //18//
Baladeva: "Surely those who are distressed and so forth are not dear to you? "Do not say so," he replies with the word "udārāḥ" (generous), because of the qualification "exceedingly.
All these—those who are distressed and the rest—are *udāra*, meaning generous or munificent.
According to Amara, *udāra* refers to a donor or one who is great.

The sense is this: those who worship me and receive from me whatever I wish to give them as their own desired object, being full of affection for me, are indeed my beloveds because they bestow much upon me.
As for the man of knowledge (*jñānī*), however, he is considered to be my very self;
for since that man of knowledge has a disciplined mind, with his thoughts surrendered to me, desiring nothing else whatsoever other than me, he is exceedingly dear to me.

Being unable to remain even for a moment without me, he has resorted to me alone as the supreme goal and reached the certainty [of this]; therefore, for me—who am likewise unable to remain even for a moment without such a one as he—he is my very self.
Nor should it be said that Hari declares non-difference from Himself regarding the soul of the knower (*jñāni-jīva*).

Because it is not established that [the Self] is an object of knowledge, because the fourfold classification of those who worship is not established, and because it would contradict the scriptural statements regarding difference in liberation;
therefore, it is called "Self" there precisely because of its extreme dearness, just as in the expression, "Bhadrasena is my self."
Others maintain that the self itself is the mind. //18//
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me, realizing, "Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great-souled person is very rare. (7.19)
Śrīdhara: He says "of many" (bahūnām) to show that such a devotee of mine is extremely rare.

Through some slight accumulation of merit over many births, in the final birth, being possessed of knowledge, one attains me—that is, one worships me—by means of the vision of the Self in all, realizing that "all this, moving and unmoving, is indeed Vāsudeva."
Therefore, that Great-Souled One, whose vision is undivided, is very difficult to find. //19//
Madhusūdana: Because it is so, therefore [it is said] "of many.

At the end of many births—those which are causes for the gradual accumulation of merit—in the final birth, which consists of the ripening of all good deeds, one becomes possessed of the knowledge that "Vāsudeva is everything" and thus takes refuge in Me, the object of unconditional love, and worships Me at all times as the sole focus of all affection.
Because, through the vision that "all this and I am Vāsudeva," all forms of love culminate in Me alone;

therefore, that great soul who possesses devotion to Me preceded by such knowledge—being one whose internal organ is utterly pure—is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), the most excellent of all, for there is no other equal to him, and none superior to him.
Consequently, he is very difficult to find among thousands of men, being impossible to obtain even with great effort.
Therefore, the meaning is that it is entirely logical that he is the object of my unsurpassed affection. //19//

Viśvanātha: You say, "I am indeed the unsurpassed goal," and therefore that knower (jñānin) attains you alone. But after how much time does that knower become eligible for devotion? To this he says: "After many...
[Vāsudeva is all]. The wise one, who perceives Vāsudeva everywhere, reaches me at the end of many births.
By virtue of such accidental association with a saintly person, one attains surrender to Me.
Such a person—a man of knowledge, a devotee, a great soul, and one of very steady mind—is extremely rare;
for it is said by Me that "among thousands of men," [only one strives for perfection].
The sense is: "What then to say of those who are single-minded devotees? They are indeed exceedingly rare. //19//
Baladeva: If it is asked, "What is the final goal for those who are distressed and so forth? he says in response, "Of many," and so on.
My devotee of the three types—such as the distressed and others—by the power of the greatness of his performed devotion, experiences many births and the highest pleasures of the senses;

then, becoming free from thirst for them, in his final birth, through association with the virtuous who know my true nature, he becomes possessed of knowledge—that is, he attains knowledge of my true nature.
"They resort to me"— this means that they thereby find [me].
He states the form of knowledge as "Vāsudeva."
Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, is indeed everything;
the meaning is that every object has its nature, existence, and activity dependent upon Kṛṣṇa.
For that which has its nature and existence dependent on another is designated as "breath" (prāṇa) or as speech and so forth in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
Indeed, they do not call them "speeches," nor "eyes," nor "ears," nor "minds"; they call them simply "breaths" (prāṇas), for the breath indeed becomes all these.
Regarding this, they say: every object is pervaded by Vāsudeva; therefore, the meaning is that "everything is Vāsudeva.
As Pārtha will later declare: "You pervade everything, and therefore You are everything" (Gītā 11.40).

For he—who, preceded by the cessation of all worldly desires, longs for Me, whose mind is exceedingly noble because his self is absorbed in Me, and who has surrendered his very self to Me—is extremely rare even among millions of the wise (*jñānin*s).
He is to be understood as possessing the characteristics described in such passages as: "This man of knowledge is dear; indeed, the man of knowledge is exceedingly dear to Me" (Gītā 7.17). //19//
Those whose wisdom has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities,
adhering to their respective rules of discipline, constrained by their own natures. (7.20)

Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that even those who are full of desire, if they worship the Supreme Lord alone for the sake of attaining their desires, they will gradually attain liberation after obtaining those desires.

However, he says in the four verses beginning with "By desires" that those who are excessively passionate (rājasa) or ignorant (tāmasa), being overwhelmed by desire, serve inferior deities and consequently transmigrate.

Those whose discrimination has been stolen away by various desires for objects such as sons, fame, or victory over enemies, worship other inferior deities, such as bhūtas, pretas, yakṣas, and so forth.
Having done what? Having undertaken each respective discipline—characterized by fasting and so forth—required for the worship of that particular deity;
and even in that regard, being constrained and brought under control by their own respective natures, that is, by the latent impressions of their previous practice. //20//

Madhusūdana: [The mind] is carried away—that is, stolen away—from Lord Vāsudeva by various petty desires and longings, such as delusion, paralyzing, attracting, subjugating, killing, and driving away, which are considered impossible to attain through service to the Blessed One; thus, having been turned away from Vāsudeva, it is directed toward minor deities who are considered to be the bestowers of those respective fruits.
Those whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is led [toward other objects] are "worshippers of other deities," meaning those who worship minor deities other than the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva;

having resorted to— that is, having relied upon— this or that specific rule (niyama), such as chanting, fasting, circumambulation, prostration, and so forth, which are well-known for the propitiation of various deities, they take refuge in [those deities], that is, they worship them, out of a desire to obtain those respective minor fruits.
Even among the minor deities, some worship only a particular one, being constrained by their own specific nature and governed by the latent impressions of their previous practice. //20//
Viśvanātha: Now, it has been understood that even those such as the distressed (ārtas) who worship You, the Blessed One, with desires, are as if their purpose is fulfilled.

But what is the fate of those distressed ones and others who worship other deities out of a desire for the removal of suffering and so forth? In response to this expectation, he says the following in four verses beginning with "With desires" (kāmair).

"Those whose knowledge has been taken away" means those whose intellects have perished, thinking that Viṣṇu does not remove the afflictions of disease and so forth as quickly as the sun and other [deities] do. "By nature" means being constrained and brought under control by their own nature; the sense is that it is their very corrupt nature that turns them away from taking refuge in me. //20//
Baladeva: Thus it has been stated that even those who worship Me with specific desires are liberated by the power of My devotion.
However, those who desire immediate happiness and worship other deities continue to transmigrate; this is what He says in the four verses beginning with "kāmair" (by desires).

Their wisdom is carried away by various desires directed toward the destruction of suffering and so forth; the meaning is that their intellect is lost because they think, "Just as the Sun and others provide the destruction of disease and such very quickly, so too does Viṣṇu."

The meaning is that each of them is restricted and constrained by their own unique nature and latent impressions (vāsanā); their very nature is such that it causes aversion toward taking refuge in Me. //20//
Whichever embodied being a devotee desires to worship with faith in whichever particular form, I ordain that very same unwavering faith for him. (7.21)

Śrīdhara: Among those who worship various particular deities, whosoever— that is, whichever devotee— desires to worship with faith whatever form, which is of the nature of a deity, as my very own manifestation, for that very devotee,
I make firm and unshakable that same faith directed toward that specific manifestation.
I am the inner controller; I ordain and I act. //21//
Madhusūdana: It should not be doubted that, by the grace of those respective deities, devotion to the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Lord of All, will arise for them as well;

for [the Lord says], "whosoever among them"—meaning, whosoever among them is desirous of a particular form, whichever deity-form they worship with faith, which has been manifested through the power of impressions from previous births, being joined with such devotion in order to worship—that is to say, to honor...
He desires and he acts.
This is the form of the root *arc* belonging to the *caurādika* class in the absence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

As the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), I establish—that is, I perform—the unwavering, firm devotion of each such seeker toward that very same divine form, which has been attained through the power of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and faith.
The meaning is not that "I bestow my own faith upon each of them";

rather, in the interpretation "that very faith," the lack of syntactic connection with the word *yat* (which) would be evident. Therefore, it has been explained by supplying the word *prati* (towards/for). //21//

Viśvanātha: Do not say that those various gods, having received worship, will become pleased and generate faith in devotion to You for the sake of the welfare of their respective worshippers; for those gods are incapable of generating even faith in devotion to themselves, let alone in devotion to Me. Thus He says: "Whosoever... (yo yaḥ).

Whichever form—such as that of the Sun or other deities—which is My own manifestation (vibhūti), I, as the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), alone bestow the very faith directed toward that specific deity for the purpose of honoring and worshipping it; it is not the deity itself that does so. //21//

Baladeva: Being the inner controller of all, possessed of great majesty, and desiring the welfare of all, I myself—intending that people should generate faith in various deities and worship them to obtain fruits corresponding to those respective forms, rather than thinking that those deities possess independent power in those matters—said "He who" in two verses:
"Whosoever among my devotees, such as those afflicted by distress and so forth, desires to worship whichever form of My body, such as Ādi (the Primordial) and others, with faith..."
For each of them, that very [devotion] directed toward their respective deity, and not directed toward me;
it is unshakable, meaning steady.
I alone ordain—that is, I produce—[the world], and not each respective deity;

and scripture declares that those various deities are my own body, as in the passage beginning: "He who dwells in the sun, yet is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.9). //21//
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [deity];
and from that [propitiation], he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone. (7.22)
Śrīdhara: And then, "by her"—that devotee, by means of that firm faith, endeavors to perform the propitiation (*ārādhana*) of her body;
and then he obtains those desires which were intended from that particular deity.
But [they were] indeed ordained and created by me alone as the inner controller (antaryāmin) of those respective deities;
for this is clear, meaning that even those respective deities are subordinate to me and are my own forms. //22//
Madhusūdana: That seeker of desire, endowed with that steady faith ordained by Me, strives to—indeed, accomplishes—the propitiation (*rādhana*) of that deity-form.
Even without a prefix, the root *rādh* signifies worship;
for if it were accompanied by a prefix, the vowel *ā* would be heard [in its place].

And then, from the presence of that deity’s body, one obtains those very desires previously intended; for this is well known: they were ordained by me alone—the omniscient bestower of the fruits of all actions, the inner controller (antaryāmin) of each respective deity—and fashioned at the time of the ripening of their respective fruits.
Or, "beneficial" and "pleasing to the mind" may be taken as a single compound.
The meaning is that even though something is harmful, it is perceived as beneficial; this refers to impermanence. //22//
Viśvanātha: "He seeks" means he performs [action]. Through the propitiation of various deities, he obtains the fruits of the propitiation of those desires.
Yet, even those various desires cannot be made full by those respective deities; thus [the Lord] says: "by Me alone ordained and fulfilled. (22)
Baladeva says: "He acts by means of that [devotion]";
he performs [action].
Therefore, from the propitiation of those various deities who have become one with my own body.

The "fruits" (kāmān) mentioned in various places are those ordained and fashioned by me alone. Although that particular worshiper may not possess such knowledge, the meaning is that I bestow the fruits, having considered that this faith is directed toward my own form. //22//
But the fruit of those of small intelligence is finite;
the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, while My devotees come to Me as well. (7.23)
Śrīdhara: Thus, although all deities are indeed my own bodies, since I am the Self of all, the worship of them is in reality the worship of me alone;
and in that regard, I myself am the bestower of the fruit.
Nevertheless, there is a disparity in the results for those who are My direct devotees and for them [the others]; thus He says, "it is finite.
For those of small intellect, whose vision is limited, even that fruit given by Me becomes finite—that is, perishable.
He explains this very point: "those who sacrifice to the gods" (devayājaḥ).
They go to the gods who are finite;
but those devoted to me attain me, who am without beginning or end, the supreme bliss. //23//

Madhusūdana: Although all deities are indeed my own bodies, as I am the Self of all, and thus the worship of them is in reality the worship of me alone—and furthermore, I alone am the inner controller who bestows the fruit in every case—nevertheless, there exists a disparity in the results for those who are directly My devotees and for those [other deities], caused by their respective discernment or lack of discernment regarding the true nature of reality. Thus, He says: "It is perishable" (antavat).

The meaning is this: for those of small intellect, who—due to their dull wisdom—are incapable of discerning the true nature of reality, and who are devotees of various respective deities, even though the fruit born from the worship of those various deities has been ordained by Me, it is indeed finite and perishable; it is not, however, an infinite fruit like that of My own discerning devotees.
Why? Because those who worship the gods—those intent on propitiating deities other than Me—reach and attain only the finite gods, such as Indra and others.
But My devotees, even if they have desires, first obtain their desired objects through My grace;
by the use of the word "api" (even), it is implied that thereafter, through the ripening of their service to Me, they attain Me, the infinite mass of bliss.
They go to, that is, they reach, even Īśvara.
Therefore, although there is equality in the state of having desires, there is a great difference between My devotees and those devoted to other deities.
Consequently, it was rightly said: "All these are indeed noble. //23//
Viśvanātha: However, the fruit for those devotees of other deities—arising from the worship of their respective deities—is finite, perishable, and temporary.

[An objection: "Granted that the labor in worship is equal, you maintain that the fruit for devotees of other deities is perishable, whereas for your own devotees it is imperishable; thus, there is this injustice in you, O Supreme Lord. To this he replies: "The worshippers of gods—the adorers of deities—go to, that is, attain, only the gods."
"Those who worship me [also reach me]";
this is the meaning.
For it is indeed a logical principle that those who worship someone certainly attain that very person.
In that regard, if even the gods are perishable, how then could their devotees be imperishable?
How much less so could the fruit of worshipping them fail to perish? For this very reason, those who are devoted to them are said to be of small intelligence.
But the Blessed Lord is eternal, His devotees are also eternal, and the fruit of devotion to Him and devotion to that devotion is likewise entirely eternal. //23//

Baladeva: If it is argued that since the gods are indeed Your own bodies, then the fruit for those who are devotees of the gods and those who are devotees of You would be the same, He says in response: "It is finite" (*antavat*).

For those of small intelligence who worship them with the notion that they are merely the sun and other deities, and not with the realization that they are My own forms, their respective fruits are small, finite, and perishable.
The sense is that, however, for those who worship Me through their body and speech, the fruit is infinite and imperishable.
For those who sacrifice to deities such as Āditya go to those very deities, who grant limited enjoyments and limited lifespans;

whereas My devotees come to Me alone—the fruit of worshipping Me, who possess eternal, immeasurable essential nature, qualities, and majesty—which is infinite and imperishable. Thus, there is a vast difference between the two. //23//
The unintelligent, not knowing my supreme nature— which is imperishable and unsurpassed— think of me, who am unmanifest, as having come into manifestation. (7.24)
Śrīdhara: If both the effort and the great distinction in the fruit are equal for us, why do all people not abandon other deities and worship you alone?
To this he says: "The unmanifest.
Those of small intellect consider me—who am unmanifest and beyond the phenomenal world—to have attained manifestation in the form of human beings, fish, tortoises, and so forth.
The reason for this is: they do not know my supreme state, which is my own essential nature;
of what kind is it?
It is imperishable and eternal.
Since there exists no state superior to that which is my own state (*mad-bhāva*),

those of dull intellect— perceiving Me, the Supreme Lord who has playfully manifested various forms of pure and powerful *sattva* for the sake of protecting the world, as being equal to other deities who possess material bodies fashioned by their own karma— do not hold Me in very high regard.
On the contrary, they resort to other deities who grant results quickly;
the meaning is that, by the manner described above, they obtain results that are finite. //24//

Madhusūdana: Although devotion to the Blessed One thus yields the supreme fruit, [the Lord] states the reason why living beings are generally averse to the Blessed One with the words, "The Unmanifest" (avyakta).
That which was "unmanifest"—existing prior to the assumption of a body due to its incapacity for activity—has now attained manifestation in the house of Vasudeva.

Those lacking intelligence and devoid of discrimination consider me, the Lord, to be merely some individual soul (jīva) who has attained the capacity for action through the limitation of a material body;

or they consider me, though unmanifest and the cause of all, to have attained manifestation— the state of being an effect— in the form of various incarnations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others.
How is it that those living beings do not discern You?
To this, he explains the reason stated as "those lacking intelligence":
they do not know My state—My essential nature—which is supreme, the form of all causes, imperishable, eternal, yet conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*).

Thus, being ignorant of my own nature— which is unconditioned, unsurpassed, the most excellent, an infinite mass of supreme bliss that is non-surpassable and non-dual— some people, observing my activities that imitate those of a living being, consider me to be merely a *jīva*.
Consequently, setting aside me whom they regard as not being the Lord, they worship some other well-known deity instead.
Therefore, the meaning is that they attain only a finite result;
and this will be stated further on: "The deluded disregard me when I have assumed a human form" (Gītā 9.11). //24//
Viśvanātha: Let alone the talk of those devoted to other deities or those of limited intellect;
even those who have studied all the scriptures, beginning with the Vedas, do not know my true nature.
Nevertheless, they [seek] Your two lotus feet, O Lord.
O Blessed One, only one who is favored by even a fragment of Your grace knows the reality of Your majesty; no other, even if searching for a long time, knows it.
Thus it was said by Brahmā as well to me.

Therefore, [the Lord] says that those of small intellect are everywhere ignorant of My true nature except for My devotees: "The unintelligent perceive Me—the very Brahman, unmanifest, beyond the phenomenal world, and formless—as having attained manifestation, birth in the house of Vasudeva, through a form consisting of Māyā."

The sense is that they think [only the illusory body is visible], because they do not know my supreme state—my true nature which transcends illusion—including my birth, deeds, pastimes, and so forth. What kind of state? [It is that which transcends illusion.]
"Avyayam" means eternal, constant, and unsurpassed, being the most excellent of all.

Regarding the word "bhāva," the *Medinīkośa* states: "Bhāva refers to existence (*sattā*), intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), intention (*abhiprāya*), activity (*ceṣṭā*), self (*ātman*), birth (*janman*), action (*kriyā*), play (*līlā*), and objects (*padārtha*)."

The eternality of the Lord’s essential nature, qualities, birth, activities, and pastimes—due to their being without beginning or end—has been established by the venerable Śrī Rūpa Gosvāmī in his work *Bhāgavatāmṛta*. Furthermore, the venerable Svāmī-pāda has stated: "My supreme state is my immutable and eternal essential nature, whose form consists of pure and exalted *sattva*. (24)

Baladeva: Now, what is the news regarding those of small intelligence who worship deities other than Me? Even though they may be proficient in the Upaniṣads, if they are devoid of devotion to Me, the realization of My true nature will not arise in them; with this intention, He says: "The Unmanifest. People who are unawakened—devoid of the intellect that perceives the reality of My true nature—regard Me, who am the Unmanifest (avyakta) because My form is the self-luminous Self and thus beyond the reach of the senses, as having attained manifestation (vyakti), [thinking] that I am an object of those [senses].

They say that I was born from Vasudeva in Devakī through an action preeminent in goodness (*sattva*), as one equal to the sons of other kings; for they, lacking association with the virtuous who know Me, do not understand My supreme, imperishable, and unsurpassed nature—
*bhāva* being used here in the senses of existence, inherent nature, intention, activity, self, or birth.
In the objects of ritual action and play, and in beings who perceive them as manifestations of power.
Thus says Medinīkāra.

The meaning is that those who are devoid of devotion to Me do not perceive My essential nature, qualities, birth, pastimes, and so forth—which are characterized as being beyond *māyā*, supreme, imperishable, eternal, unsurpassed, and the best of all—but instead grasp them as being otherwise: illusory, impermanent, and common.
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Hari consists solely of the essence of knowledge and bliss, as indicated by such passages as "Brahman is knowledge and bliss.

His multitude of qualities, such as omniscience and so forth, are inherent to that essential nature, being composed of infinite auspicious attributes, as indicated by such passages as "He is the Self of infinite auspicious qualities.
His "birth" is merely a manifestation, as indicated by such passages as "Though he is unborn, yet..."
But for those who worship Him, the Unmanifested alone becomes manifest by His very grace—as stated in such passages as:
"O Bṛhaspati, He cannot be seen by you or by us;
only he whom He favors is indeed worthy to see Him. //24//
I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā; deluded by this, the world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable. 7.25.
Śrīdhara: He states the reason for their own ignorance with the words "I am not":
"I am not manifest (*prakāśa*), that is, I do not appear clearly, to the entire world; rather, [I am manifest] only to those who are My devotees."
Because he was shrouded by *yoga-māyā*;
*yoga* is my own certain, inconceivable play of wisdom (*prajñā*),
so called because it is exceedingly skillful in the fashioning and manifestation of *māyā*.
Enveloped by that [ignorance], and therefore being deluded regarding the knowledge of my true nature, this world does not know me, who am unborn and immutable. //25//

Madhusūdana said: "Indeed, at the time of His birth, He manifested that very divine form residing in Śrī Vaikuṇṭha which is meditated upon by all yogis; and now, He is endowed with divine ornaments such as the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, the forest garland, the crown, and earrings; He possesses four arms bearing the conch, lotus, Kaumodakī mace, and the discus; He has the glorious Garuḍa as His vehicle; and He is the object of great majesty, such as the royal consecration as the Lord of Lords performed by the entire world of the gods."
To Him who conquers all gods and demons; whose nature is the graceful play of various divine pastimes; the crest-jewel of all incarnations; the manifest Lord of Vaikuṇṭha;

who descended to the earth for the deliverance from the suffering of all worlds; the very embodiment of the essence of unsurpassed beauty, which cannot be produced even by the creative power of Brahmā;
who bewildered the Creator with His childhood sports; who wears divine yellow garments as radiant as the rays of the sun; the incomparable Śyāmasundara.

In You—who defeated Indra for the sake of the *pārijāta* tree taken by force; who conquered Śiva, the moon-crested Lord, in a battle with arrows; who stripped away the life-force and all possessions of the multitude of great *daityas* such as Naraka, who were victors over all gods and demons; who bestowed supreme opulence upon the most wretched of men like Śrīdāma; who assume sixteen thousand divine forms; who possess immeasurable weight of virtues;
who are of great majesty; and who are praised by hosts of great sages such as Nārada and Mārkaṇḍeya—how could even one lacking discrimination [not seek refuge]?
Desiring to dispel Arjuna’s doubt—namely, whether he perceives Him as a human being or as a living soul—the Blessed One says, "I am not.
The intention is: "I am not manifest in my own form to the whole world;
however, I am manifest to certain of My devotees."

To the question of how He is not manifest to the entire world, He states the reason: "He is veiled by *yoga-māyā*. *Yoga* is My volition (*saṅkalpa*), and *māyā* is that which operates under its control; thus, *yoga-māyā* is the *māyā* that conforms to such a volition, namely: "Let this person who is not a devotee not know Me in My true nature. Being thoroughly veiled by this *māyā*, even though the causes for knowledge exist, he has been rendered unfit to become an object of knowledge.
Therefore, regarding what was said—that they do not know my supreme nature—it is meant that my own resolve alone is the cause.

Consequently, the meaning is this: being deluded by My māyā and having their knowledge veiled, these people, who are distinct from the four kinds of devotees, even though the cause for knowledge exists, perceive Me—the unborn, undecaying, beginningless, endless Supreme Lord—as merely some human being due to their perverted vision.
It is well known even in the world that [māyā] conceals the true nature of an existing object and displays something that does not exist. //25//
Viśvanātha: Now, if you are indeed eternal in form, qualities, and pastimes, then why is such an all-time state of yours not perceived? To this, he replies: "I am not... [and so forth].

I am neither manifest nor visible to all people existing in all places and times; for although I am always resplendent, possessing qualities, pastimes, and a retinue, I appear only occasionally and only to certain individuals within certain cosmic eggs. Furthermore, just as the sun is not always visible to the world due to the obstruction of Mount Sumeru, [so too am I].
But at certain times,

I too am similarly veiled by *yogamāyā*. And although the sun, situated within the sphere of light (*jyotiścakra*), shines perpetually and universally in the midst of that sphere for all living beings as it revolves, [it is not perceived] by people existing in all times and places.
He is not manifest [to everyone];
rather, He is visible only to those people residing in occasional regions such as Bhārata and others, and I am likewise so.

Just as the sun of one's own true nature (svarūpa) is always visible within one's own abodes, even so, Kṛṣṇa residing there is visible to the people of the present day who dwell in Mathurā, Dvārakā, and other abodes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
How is it that He is not seen?
It is said: if Mount Sumeru were situated in the midst of the circle of luminaries, then the sun, being obscured by it, would not be visible.

However, in that abode of Kṛṣṇa—the sun among men—such as Mathurā and other places, Yoga-māyā alone always resides in the position of Mount Sumeru; therefore, the sun of Kṛṣṇa, being obscured by her, is never seen.
But this is only at certain times; thus, everything is faultless.
Therefore, the deluded world does not recognize me—who am Śyāmasundara in form, the son of Vasudeva, the imperishable, and devoid of illusory birth and the like.
For this very reason, even after ultimately abandoning me, who am an ocean of auspicious qualities, they worship Brahman alone, whose essential nature is non-different from mine. //25//
Baladeva: But surely both devotees and non-devotees perceive You through Your very grace; since You are manifested only for those who worship You, how is this so?
To that he says: "I am not...
It is only for the devotees that I—whose nature is a mass of eternal consciousness and bliss, and who possess infinite auspicious qualities and activities—am manifest and revealed.
But this is not so for all, even for those who are not devotees;
for I am "enveloped by yoga-māyā," which means my surroundings are covered by that māyā characterized by the yoga of deluding those who are averse to Me.
As it has been said: "Obeisance to Brahman, whose majesty is concealed by the curtain of māyā."
Deluded by Māyā, this world does not recognize me, whose power surpasses that of humans and gods, and who am even worshipped by Brahmā, Rudra, and others.
Of what nature am I? I am "unborn," meaning devoid of birth; and because I am "imperishable," my essential nature, power, omniscience, and so forth have never fallen away—this is the meaning. //25//
I know all beings that have passed away, those that are present, O Arjuna, and those yet to come; but no one knows Me.

Śrīdhara: It was stated that [others] do not know My nature, which is the supreme of all. Demonstrating that very supremacy of His own through the power of unobstructed knowledge, He declares the ignorance of others with the words "I know" (vedāham). I know—that is, I am aware of—all beings existing in the three periods of time: those past and destroyed, those present, and those future and yet to come; indeed, all beings, both stationary and moving.
This is well known because my [nature] has illusion as its substratum, whereas that [illusion] lacks the power to delude its own substratum. However,
some do not know me at all, because they are deluded by my illusion.
For it is well known in the world that illusion depends upon its own substratum and that it causes delusion to others. //26//
Madhusūdana says: Therefore, because He can delude everyone through His own independent *māyā*, and because His own knowledge is unobstructed, He says, "I know.

Though I am the one whose all-encompassing knowledge is unimpeded and who deludes all the worlds by means of *māyā*, I know all beings—those that have passed away and long since perished, those that are present, and those yet to be;
thus, I know all beings existing in the three periods of time, whether stationary or moving.
"O Arjuna, therefore there is no doubt that I am omniscient and the Supreme Lord"— this is the meaning. But as for me...
The word "tu" (but) is intended to highlight the obstruction to knowledge.
Even though I am all-seeing, someone—deluded by My Māyā—does not know Me, who am like a magician, except for My devotee who is the recipient of My grace; this is because they are deluded by My Māyā.
Therefore, the intention is that, precisely due to the absence of knowledge of My true nature, living beings generally do not worship Me. //26//

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, because Māyā deludes its own substratum, it is "external" (bahir-aṅgā); whereas Yoga-māyā is "internal" (antaraṅgā) and does not veil my knowledge. Thus he says, "I know [all]" (vedāham). But no one—neither the worldly folk, whether ordinary or extraordinary, nor even Mahārudra and others who are all-knowing—knows me in my entirety.
The meaning is that [the soul is bound] by illusion (māyā) and by the power of yoga-illusion (yogamāyā), respectively, due to the obscuration of knowledge (jñānāvaraṇa). //26//
Baladeva: If it is argued that, because you are veiled by *māyā*, you would fall into a state of ignorance like that of a *jīva*, he replies with the words "I know [Him].
The meaning is: there is no modification whatsoever in Me due to *māyā*, which—though dependent on Me and overwhelmed by My splendor—serves Me from afar like a curtain.
Furthermore, the meaning of "He knows Me" is that such a knower of Mine is extremely rare even among millions. //26//
O descendant of Bharata, O scorcher of foes, all beings fall into delusion at birth due to the confusion caused by the pairs of opposites arising from desire and hatred. (7.27)
Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that the ignorance of living beings regarding the Supreme Lord is due to their being objects of Māyā.
He states the cause for the firmness of that very ignorance with the word "iccha" (desire).
That which is created is "sarga" (creation).
When creation— that is, the production of a gross body— has occurred, there arises a desire favorable to it and an aversion toward what is unfavorable to it.

From these two, there arises (samuttha) or is produced that delusion (moha), which consists of the loss of discrimination caused by the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and so forth.
Therefore, all beings fall into delusion;
they develop an even more intense attachment, thinking, "I alone am happy" or "I am suffering.
Consequently, because they lack knowledge of Me, they do not resort to Me—this is the sense. //27//

Madhusūdana: Regarding *yoga-māyā*, he states another cause for the obstruction of the knowledge of the true nature of the Lord (*bhagavat-tattva*), which consists of an intense identification with the aggregate of the body and senses, preceded by an attachment to enjoyment: "By desire...

By means of desire and aversion toward objects that are favorable or unfavorable, there arises delusion (*moha*) caused by the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, etc.; through this delusion—characterized by the misconception "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth—all beings fall into a state of confusion, which is an incapacity for discrimination (*viveka*).
When creation occurs— that is, when the production of a gross body takes place— they go [to it],
O Bhārata,
O scorcher of foes!

The sense is this: by virtue of the greatness of your lineage and the power of your own nature, as expressed in these two addresses, the enemy known as the delusion of duality is not able to overcome you;
for there is no living being whatsoever that is free from desire and aversion, nor is knowledge of external objects possible for one who is possessed by those two.
How much more so, then, regarding Me as their own self?

Therefore, because their inner faculties are agitated by passion and hatred, all beings do not recognize Me, the Supreme Lord, who has become their very self; consequently, they do not worship Me, even though I am worthy of worship. //27//

Viśvanātha: In response to the inquiry as to from what time living beings have been deluded by that Māyā, he says, "Desire," and so forth. At the time of *sarga*—the commencement of the creation of the universe—all beings, that is, all living beings, become utterly bewildered.
By what means? By desire and aversion awakened by past karma; specifically, desire is the longing for an object favorable to the senses.

Aversion toward what is disagreeable; the dualities arising from and produced by those two—namely, honor and dishonor, cold and heat and so forth, pleasure and pain, and the delusion regarding women and men, such as: "I am honored, I am happy," or "I am insulted, I am miserable."
Through that delusion consisting of ignorance— which takes such forms as "this woman is mine" or "this man is mine"— they attain *saṃmoha*, which is extreme attachment to wives, sons, and so forth.
For this very reason, those who are thus excessively attached have no qualification for devotion to Me.
As I myself shall say to Uddhava:
"But for that man who, by chance, has developed faith in my stories and the like,
neither despondent nor overly attached, the yoga of devotion bestows perfection upon him" (BhP 11.20.8).
Baladeva says: "Why is your knower so very difficult to find? To this he replies with the word "icchet" (one who desires).
At the very time of creation, at the moment of their own birth, all beings fall into delusion.
He asks, "By what? and replies, "By the delusion of the pairs of opposites."

The meaning is: by that delusion characterized by attachment—consisting of honor and dishonor, pleasure and pain, and the pairs of woman and man—which [manifests as] "I am honored, may I be happy; but if dishonored, I shall be miserable," or "this is my wife," "this is my husband.

To the question "By what kind [of delusion]?", he says: "by desire..."—meaning that in whatever place and to whatever extent desire and aversion existed in a previous birth, they persist in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and from these one arises in a subsequent birth in those very places.
In this context, "is produced" is the meaning.
"Desire" is attachment (*rāga*).
Thus, because all beings are utterly deluded, one who possesses My knowledge is very difficult to find. //27//
But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end— they, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship Me with firm resolve. (7.28)
Śrīdhara: Why, then, are some seen worshipping you?
To this he says: "Of those...

Those whose evil, which is the obstacle to all [virtue], has reached its end and perished—being of virtuous conduct and character, liberated from the delusion caused by the pairs of opposites, firm in their vows, and being single-minded devotees—[they worship me].
They devote themselves. //28//
Madhusūdana: If all beings fall into delusion, how then is it said that "four kinds [of people] worship Me"?
True; because their sins have been destroyed by the excellence of their virtuous deeds, He says, "Of whom... [referring to the verse beginning with *yeṣām*].

But for those people who are unlike others in the world— whose births are fruitful, whose deeds are meritorious, and who have been habituated to the practice of virtue throughout many lifetimes— for them, by those various meritorious actions, the sin that obstructs knowledge has reached its end, its final conclusion; and through the absence of that sin, they are free from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, which is the source of error such as attachment and aversion.

Those of firm vows, whose resolve is unshakable, being naturally liberated and having abandoned [all else] by virtue of their unfitness for returning, possess a cognition free from any suspicion regarding its invalidity—generated by authoritative means—that "the Blessed Lord alone is to be worshipped, and He is of such-and-such a nature. Being without any other refuge, they worship and serve Me, the Supreme Self; it is only such as these who, being of four kinds, worship.
In this context, those referred to by the word "sukṛtin" (those of virtuous deeds) are designated as "me.
Therefore, the general rule (utsarga) is that all beings fall into delusion;
however, among them, those who are virtuous, being free from delusion, worship me—this is the exception (apavāda), and thus there is no contradiction.
This very principle was previously established in the verse beginning with "by means of the three states consisting of the gunas";
therefore, the sense is that one must always strive to accumulate meritorious actions that purify the sattva. //28//

Viśvanātha: If so, who then possesses the qualification for devotion? To this he says: "For those whose sinful karma has reached its end"—that is, its limit or state of destruction, but not yet completely destroyed. When the quality of *sattva* increases in them, there is a decrease of the quality of *tamas*.
When that [discrimination] exists, the delusion that is its effect also diminishes.
When delusion has diminished, they indeed become free from excessive attachment and worship Me through association with My devotees who act according to their own will (*yādṛcchika*).

However, those whose sins have been completely destroyed through the practice of worship and so forth, being liberated from delusion without remainder, firm in their vows and having attained the ultimate goal, worship Me.
Nor should it be thought that meritorious action alone is the cause of both forms of devotion;
for one might not attain [the Lord], even with great effort, through yoga, Sāṅkhya, charity, vows, austerity, sacrifice, exposition, study, or renunciation. (BhP 11.12.9)
Thus it is stated by the Blessed One;
for it has been demonstrated in many ways that for pure devotional yoga (*kevala-bhakti-yoga*), the performance of meritorious deeds and the like is not at all a cause. //28//

Baladeva said: "If it is argued that devotion to You is not perceived in some beings because of the statement that 'all beings fall into delusion at the time of creation,' he replies to that: for those living beings whose sins have reached their end and attained destruction through the accidental falling of the glance of the Great One (Mahattama), the beings of Viṣṇu indeed move about for the purification of all beings."
This is according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*).

To the question "Of what kind?", he says: "Puṇya... etc. "Puṇya" refers to their meritorious and pleasing action, which consists in the beholding of the Supreme Lord; for Amara states: "The word *puṇya* may also mean beautiful."
Firm in their vows, having attained steadfastness through association with the great, and being liberated from the delusion of dualities, those who know the truth of My nature worship Me. //28//
Those who strive, taking refuge in Me for liberation from old age and death, they know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self (adhyātma), and all action in its entirety. 7.29
Śrīdhara: And thus, he says "jarā" etc., [meaning] that those who worship Me in this way, having realized everything that is to be known, become successful in their purpose.
Those who, taking refuge in Me, strive for liberation—that is, for the removal—of old age and death, they know That Supreme Brahman;
and they know the entirety of the inner self (adhyātma).
The meaning is that they know the pure Self, which is distinct from the body and so forth, as that by which [liberation] is to be attained;
and the meaning is that they know all action, together with its secret essence, as the means for attaining that. //29//
Madhusūdana: Now, in order to rouse Arjuna’s inquiry, two verses are stated as the "threads" (sūtra) [of the teaching].
The subsequent chapter will serve as the "exegesis" (vṛtti) for these very two.

[They concern those] who are disenchanted with the sufferings of saṃsāra and seek liberation from old age and death—that is, for the removal of the various unbearable sufferings of saṃsāra such as old age, death, and so forth.

Having taken refuge in me— the Blessed One who possesses all qualities— as the sole cause of that [world], turning away from everything else, they strive and strive; performing prescribed actions dedicated to me and free from desire for fruits, their internal organs (minds) gradually become purified, and they perceive me as the pure, supreme cause of that world, the substratum of *māyā*.

They know me as Brahman, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), which is the indicated meaning (lakṣya) of that state; and they know all actions—beginning with approaching a guru, hearing, and reflecting—which are the means for realizing both of those [Brahman and the qualified Lord], to be entirely unfailing in their result. This is the meaning. //29//

Viśvanātha: Thus, having stated that these three types of devotees—the distressed and the others—who worship Me with desire become successful in their aims, whereas those who worship other deities fall, the Blessed Lord has also described those who are qualified even if they do not worship Him. Now, He says "jare" (in old age) to show that there is yet another fourth type of My devotee who possesses desire.

The meaning is that those yogins who strive, exert themselves for the liberation—that is, the destruction—of old age and death; that is to say, those who desire liberation worship Me. They [perceive] that well-known Brahman, as well as the entire Self existing as the enjoyer with respect to the body.

Through the power of devotion to Me alone, they know the inner individual soul, all its actions, and the cycle of worldly existence for the living being produced by those various kinds of actions. //29//

Baladeva: Thus it has been stated that my devotees who possess desires—such as those seeking relief from distress and so forth—attain Me after experiencing their desires; whereas those who worship deities other than Me continue to transmigrate.
Now, it is said that there is yet another type of My devotee with desires, namely "the aged," and so on:
those who, desiring only liberation from old age and death, take refuge in Me and strive by performing My worship.
They perform prostrations and other such acts toward Him;
they know that well-known Brahman in its entirety along with its adjuncts, and they know the entire field of the self (adhyātma) as well as action (karma).
The meanings of the terms "Brahmā" and so forth, as well as the terms "the elemental" (adhibhūta) and so forth, will be explained by the Blessed One Himself in the subsequent chapter.

The meaning is that by the service of my worship, those who possess discernment attain liberation after having realized [the truth], but not my state of being beloved, which brings one under my control.
And thus the Smṛti says: "O dear one, when she once bestowed the path of the Bhāgavatas, consisting of silence and devoid of any other self," and so forth. (29)
Those who know Me as the Adhibhūta (the presiding deity over the elements), the Adhidaiva (the presiding deity over the gods), and the Adhiyajña (the presiding deity over sacrifice)— they,
with concentrated minds, know Me even at the time of death.
Śrīdhara: Nor is there even a suspicion of a fall from yoga for those who are thus situated; therefore, he says, "together with the adhibhūta," and so forth.
The Blessed Lord Himself will explain the meaning of the terms *adhibhūta* and the others in the subsequent chapter.

Those who know Me together with the *adhibhūta*, the *adhidaiva*, and the *adhiyajña*, they are possessed of disciplined minds—those whose minds are attached to Me—and they know Me even at the time of departure, even at the moment of death.
They know [this], yet even so, they do not become distracted and forget me;
therefore, the sense is that for my devotees there is no fear of falling away from yoga. //30//
"By those devoted to Kṛṣṇa, the knowledge of Brahman is attained without effort"; thus, for the sake of the yoga of realization, it has been fully elucidated in the seventh [chapter].
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Yoga of Knowledge," in the *Subodhinī*, a commentary on the *Bhagavad-gītā* composed by the venerable Śrīdhara Svāmī.
Madhusūdana: Nor should it be suspected that My devotees, being of such a nature, would forget Me even at the time of death due to the loss of control over their senses;

for those who know Me as being with the *adhibhūta* and *adhidaiva*—that is, together with the *adhibhūta* and *adhidaiva*—and likewise as being with the *adhiyajña*, together with the *adhiyajña*, they possess concentrated minds, meaning their minds are always absorbed in Me.

The virtuous, due to the intensity of those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), at the time of departure— that is, at the time of the exit of the vital breath— even when the aggregate of the senses is in a state of extreme agitation,
know Me, the Self of all, without effort indeed by My grace;
for even at the time of their death, the mental modification takes on My very form due to the intensity of the impressions previously accumulated.
And thus, the sense is that they have indeed achieved their purpose through the yoga of devotion to Me.

The Blessed Lord will explain the terms *adhibhūta*, *adhidaiva*, and *adhiyajña* in the subsequent chapter following Arjuna’s inquiry; therefore, everything is clear. Thus, here, with respect to the person of superior qualification, that which is to be known (*jñeya*), and with respect to the person of middling qualification, that which is to be meditated upon (*dhyeya*)—namely, Brahman as denoted by the word "That" (*tat-pada*)—has been defined through both secondary (*lakṣaṇā*) and primary (*mukhyā*) functions.

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of Brahman, the Reality to be Known and Meditated Upon According to the Different Qualifications of the Seeker," in the *Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītā-Gūḍhārtha-Dīpikā* composed by Śrī Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, disciple of the feet of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrī Viśveśvara Sarasvatī.

Viśvanātha: By the power of devotion to Me, those who possess such knowledge of Me as this shall have that very same knowledge even at the time of their end; they do not have a mind like others, which—brought about by karma—is in accordance with the acquisition of a future body. Thus He says, "sādhibhūta" (along with the elemental beings), etc. The terms *adhibhūta* and so forth will be explained in the following chapter.
Only those devotees who know the reality of Hari cross over Māyā;
they are said here to be of six kinds—thus the meaning of the chapter has been explained. //30//
Thus, in this delightful commentary that showers the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted, the seventh chapter of the Gītā has been appropriately concluded for the virtuous. 7.
Baladeva: Furthermore, he says "sādhu" (well) to show that the knowledge of Him attained through such service never falls away.

Those who know Me—accompanied by the Adhibhūta, the Adhidaiva, and the Adhiyajña—meaning they understand Me through association with the virtuous (*sat-prasaṅga*), they know Me even at the time of departure, at the moment of death; the meaning is that they do not forget Me, unlike others who are distracted. //30//
Those devotees who know me in truth cross over my māyā;
they, moreover, are of five kinds—this is the definitive conclusion regarding the seventh.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the commentary on the Śrīmad-Bhagavad-gītā Upaniṣad.
